王學孔〔貫江西吉安府安福縣民籍，國子生，治易經，字魯卿，行二十九，年三十八，七月十二日生〕。曾祖循義〔壽官〕，祖翀，父秩，母劉氏。慈侍下，兄學閔、學曾、學孟、學臯、學夔〔吏部郎中〕，弟學舜、學益〔主事〕，娶劉氏。江西鄉試第三十一名，會試第一百三十七名。

萬義〔貫直隸山海衛軍籍，江西奉新縣人，衛學生，治易經，字質夫，行二，年三十五，十一月十六日生〕。曾祖能，祖全，父貴，嫡母馬氏，生母余氏。永感下，兄仁，娶張氏。順天府鄉試第四十五名，會試第三百二十八名。
translation_en:
Liu Geng, courtesy name Botian, was registered in an official household in Lanzhou, Lintao Prefecture, Shaanxi, with ancestral origins in Ninghua County, Fujian. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Rites, he ranked first in family birth order, was aged thirty-nine, and was born on the eighteenth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Rong; his grandfather, Yi, was posthumously appointed Deputy Office Director in the Court of Imperial Entertainments; and his father, Yu, was a Department Magistrate. His father's former wife, née Han, received the title Lady for Service; his mother was née Zhang. His father was deceased and his mother living. His younger brothers were Yun and Zi, and his wife was née Han (漢). He placed fifth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 184th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Xingzhong, courtesy name Weishen, was registered in a civilian household in Tongzhou, Shuntian Prefecture. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked first in family birth order, was aged thirty-five, and was born on the tenth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xiu, his grandfather Li, and his father Bian; his mother was née Lu and his stepmother née Ma. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Xingzhi, Xingshize, Xingjin, Xingshiyong, Xinggong, Xingshitai, Xingshu, Xingshiheng, Xingjian, Xingjing, and Xingren. His wife was née Jia. He placed twenty-eighth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 241st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Xuekong, courtesy name Luqing, was registered in a civilian household in Anfu County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked twenty-ninth in family birth order, was aged thirty-eight, and was born on the twelfth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather, Xunyi, held an honorary official title granted for longevity; his grandfather was Chong, his father Zhi, and his mother née Liu. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Xuemin, Xuezeng, Xuemeng, Xuegao, and Xuekui, the last a Bureau Director in the Ministry of Personnel. His younger brothers were Xueshun and Xueyi, the latter a Secretary. His wife was née Liu. He placed thirty-first in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 137th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wan Yi, courtesy name Zhifu, was registered in a military household of Shanhai Guard in the Metropolitan Region, with ancestral origins in Fengxin County, Jiangxi. A student of the guard school specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked second in family birth order, was aged thirty-five, and was born on the sixteenth day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Neng, his grandfather Quan, and his father Gui; his legal mother was née Ma and his birth mother née Yu. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Ren, and his wife was née Zhang. He placed forty-fifth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 328th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Li Yizhuang, registered in a civilian household in Nanhai County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, was a National University student specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Zhida; he ranked thirtieth in family order and was aged thirty-six [?]; he was born on the eighteenth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zheng, his grandfather Jun, his father Chunfang, and his mother née Chen. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Dong (Department Magistrate), Yizhen, and Yifu; his younger brother was Yitai. He married a woman née Chen. He placed twentieth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and fifty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Lan, registered in a military household of Dezhou Guard in the Metropolitan Region and a native of Huating County, was a National University student specializing in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Mengguan; he ranked fourth in family order, was aged thirty-six, and was born on the sixth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jingxian, his grandfather Li, and his father Xian; his father's former wife was née Du, and his mother was née Gao. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His elder brothers were Hong and Ji; his younger brother was Run. He married a woman née Li. He placed seventh in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 104th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Luo Ang, registered in a military household in Sanyuan County, Xi'an Prefecture, Shaanxi, was a National University student specializing in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Zhongmian; he ranked first in family order, was aged forty-two, and was born on the fifteenth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Kuan, his grandfather You (an honorary official honored for longevity), his father Jing, and his mother née Wang. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His younger brothers were Ze and Zheng. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed fifty-second in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 334th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shen Nanjin, registered in an artisan household in Qiantang County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was the Instructor of the county school in Wanzai, Jiangxi, and specialized in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Ziqing; he ranked first in family order, was aged forty, and was born on the twenty-ninth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jingyang, his grandfather Zongshou, and his father Jun; his father's former wife was née Zhu, and his mother was née Wei. Both parents were deceased. His younger brothers were Zhongjin, Mingjin, and Yingjin. He married a woman née Chen and subsequently married another woman née Chen. He placed seventeenth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 389th in the Metropolitan Examination.

王鴻漸〔貫河南南陽府南陽縣軍籍，國子生，治書經，字懋德，行二，年四十九，五月初二日生〕。曾祖道十，祖覺成〔贈通議大夫吏部右侍郎〕，父本〔贈通議大夫吏部右侍郎〕，母司氏〔贈淑人〕。永感下，兄鴻儒〔南京戶部尚書，謚文莊〕，娶呂氏。河南鄉試第一名，會試第三百十六名。

translation_en:
Zhang Yuanxiao 張元孝, registered in a civilian household in Ruyang County, Runing Prefecture, Henan, was a prefectural government student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Zhongli; he ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-two years old, born on the eighteenth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Tong, his grandfather Tai, and his father Lun; his father's former wife was née Chen, and his mother was née You. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yuanzhong, Yuanqing, and Yuanfu. He married a woman née Zhao. He placed second in the Henan Provincial Examination and 265th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Bian Yanluo 邊彥駱, registered in a military household in Qi County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Guolong; he ranked ninth among his brothers and was thirty-eight years old, born on the twenty-eighth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was He; his grandfather Tong was granted the title of Investigating Censor; and his father You held the honorary designation of Philanthropic Official. His legal mother and his birth mother were both née Wang. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His elder brothers were Yanwei, a County Office Manager; Yanqi; Yancong, a student of the Directorate of Education; Yanjun; Yanhua, a Director of Food Services; Yanxiang, an official awaiting selection for appointment; and Yanliu. His younger brothers were Yanzhou, a Director of Food Services, and Yanli. He married a woman née Chu. He placed seventeenth in the Henan Provincial Examination and seventy-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Hongjian 王鴻漸, registered in a military household in Nanyang County, Nanyang Prefecture, Henan, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Classic of Documents. His courtesy name was Maode; he ranked second among his brothers and was forty-nine years old, born on the second day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Daoshi. His grandfather Juecheng and his father Ben were each posthumously granted the titles of Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Right Vice Minister of Personnel. His mother, née Si, was posthumously granted the title of Lady of Gentleness. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother Hongru was Minister of Revenue at Nanjing, with the posthumous name Wenzhuang. He married a woman née Lü. He placed first in the Henan Provincial Examination and 316th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Huang Cheng 黃澄, registered in a military household in Nan'an County, Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian, was a county government student specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Tingsu; he ranked second among his brothers and was forty years old, born on the third day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Min, his grandfather Yi, and his father Deping; his mother was née Zhuang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Yuan, and his younger brothers were Qing and Ying. He married a woman née Li. He placed forty-third in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 200th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Li Xunyi, registered in Yin County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Shixing. Ranked third in birth order, he was thirty-seven sui and was born on the thirteenth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xidi, his grandfather Duan, his father Zhenghua, and his mother née He. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Xunren; his younger brothers were Xunli, Xunzhi, Xunxin, and Xundao. He married a woman née Liu. He placed seventy-third in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and ninety-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Shiheng, registered in Anyi County, Jie Subprefecture, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, belonged to an artisan household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Jiahui. Ranked second in birth order, he was thirty-three sui and was born on the sixth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Rong, his grandfather Wei, and his father Xiong. His father's former wives were née Gao and née Hou; his mother was née Zhou, and his stepmother née Sun. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Liangchen; his younger brothers were Shizheng, Shitai, and Shijian. He married a woman née Lü. He placed twenty-sixth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 242nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Xiang, registered in Xinhui County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, belonged to a military household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Junan. Ranked fourth in birth order, he was forty-five sui and was born on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Qiuhua, his grandfather Fuyi, his father Deyou (holder of an honorary official title for longevity), and his mother née Lu. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Han (a School Recorder), Yi, and Qiao. He married a woman née Chen. He placed twenty-sixth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and eighty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hu Xiang, registered in Neixiang County, Deng Subprefecture, Nanyang Prefecture, Henan, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Jizhi. Ranked first in birth order, he was thirty-eight sui and was born on the twenty-second day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ji; his grandfather Zhong was granted the title of Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Rites; his father Rui was Right Vice Censor-in-chief of the Censorate; and his mother, née Li, was granted the title of Lady (ruren). His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brother was Hong (an Instructor in Medicine); his younger brothers were Han (a tribute scholar), Pan, and Yang. He married a woman née Shi 史 and subsequently women née Liu and née Shi 時. He placed sixth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 182nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Xie Biao 謝表, of Changshu County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was registered in a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Zhengzi. Ranked first in his family, he was aged forty-two and was born on the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Qi, his grandfather Yong, and his father Yuanyou〔holder of an honorary official title for longevity〕; his mother was née Xu. His father was living and his mother deceased. His younger brothers were Gun and Pou, and he married a woman née Hu. He placed 102nd in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 220th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhu Jie 朱節, of Wu County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was registered in a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Quanfu. Ranked first in his family, he was aged thirty-three and was born on the thirtieth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Lu, his grandfather Jun, and his father Qian; his mother was née Chen. His parents and grandparents were living. His elder brother was Hongjian〔a metropolitan graduate (jinshi)〕, and his younger brothers were Kun, Heng, Jian, Lin, Sui, and Jiji. He married a woman née Shen. He placed twelfth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 208th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Qiao Ying 喬英, of Shulu County, Qizhou, Baoding Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was registered in a civilian household and was a county government school student. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Bocang. Ranked fifth in his family, he was aged forty-one and was born on the twelfth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shizhong, his grandfather Qing, and his father Shen〔holder of an honorary official title for longevity〕; his father's former wife was née Zhang, and his mother was née Jia. Both his parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Kuan, Wen, Ju, and Quan, and his younger brother was Jun. He married a woman née Ren and subsequently a woman née Zhou. He placed fortieth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and seventieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Dong 楊東, of Dangtu County, Taiping Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, was registered in a military household and was a prefectural government school student. He specialized in the Classic of Poetry; his courtesy name was Qiming. Ranked first in his family, he was aged thirty-one and was born on the third day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Hong, his grandfather Mian, and his father Yan; his mother was née Gong. Both his parents were living. His younger brother was Ce, and he married a woman née Liu. He placed ninety-first in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and ninety-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

吳玼〔貫浙江杭州府錢塘縣民籍，府學生，治禮記，字汝瑩，行十一，年四十六，正月初二日生〕。曾祖原敬〔贈通議大夫都察院右副都御史〕，祖士寧〔贈通議大夫都察院右副都御史〕，父誠〔南京兵部尚書〕，前母萬氏、李氏，嫡母莫氏，生母周氏。慈侍下，兄璿〔府同知〕、璽、瑞、珍、琳、璋〔義官〕、玭、琠、瑤〔中書舍人〕、瓊，弟珂、璵〔貢士〕、珊，娶王氏。浙江鄉試第十七名，會試第一百二十三名。
translation_en:
Wang Liu 王旒, registered in a military household in Jiyang County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Chengyu; he ranked third in birth order and was aged forty-two, born on the first day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Caixing, his grandfather Bin, and his father Jing; his mother was née Zhuang and his stepmother née Li. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Yue and Sen, and his younger brothers Zhu and Wei. He married a woman née Liu and subsequently a woman née Li. He placed forty-fourth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 317th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhu Shou 朱綬, registered in a civilian household in Nanzheng County, Hanzhong Prefecture, Shaanxi, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Chaoyi; he ranked second in birth order and was aged forty-three, born on the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Youcheng, a County Magistrate; his grandfather was Xun; and his father was Chongzheng, a County Vice Magistrate. His mother was née Zhang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Zhang, an honorary official, and his younger brother Ji. He married a woman née Wang. He placed thirty-first in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 184th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Fu E 傅鶚, registered in a civilian household in Xinyu County, Linjiang Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Wenrui; he ranked second in birth order and was aged thirty, born on the second day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Xunzi, his grandfather Jieying, and his father Lizhou; his father's former wife was née Liao and his mother née Liu. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Jirui and Chaorui, and his younger brother Hong. He married a woman née Ruan and subsequently a woman née Zong. He placed fiftieth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 336th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Ci 吳玼, registered in a civilian household in Qiantang County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a prefectural school student specializing in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Ruying; he ranked eleventh in birth order and was aged forty-six, born on the second day of the first month. His great-grandfather Yuanjing and grandfather Shining were each posthumously granted the titles Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Right Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate. His father Cheng was Minister of War at Nanjing. His father's former wives were née Wan and née Li; his legal mother was née Mo and his birth mother née Zhou. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Xuan, a Prefectural Vice Prefect; Xi; Rui; Zhen; Lin; Zhang, an honorary official; Pin; Tian; Yao, a Central Secretariat Drafter; and Qiong. His younger brothers were Ke; Yu, a tribute scholar; and Shan. He married a woman née Wang. He placed seventeenth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 123rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
He Zhi, courtesy name Dezheng, was registered in a civilian household in Jinxian County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi. A county school student specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked fourth in his family and was aged thirty-two, born on the sixteenth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Jiujiang, his grandfather Jue, his father Ji, and his mother née Shu. His mother was living and his father deceased. He married a woman née Zhao. He placed sixth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 271st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zheng Lian, courtesy name Shizhou, was registered in a civilian household in Jiangning County, Yingtian Prefecture, and was a native of Xinjian County, Jiangxi. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked first in his family and was aged twenty-three, born on the twenty-fifth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Sigong, posthumously appointed Assistant Prefect; his grandfather Li, a Prefect; his father Min, holder of a seventh-rank prestige title; and his mother née Ouyang. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yi, He, Han, and Qu. He married a woman née Zhao and subsequently women née Yu 俞 and Yu 宇. He placed thirty-third in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 280th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Gun, courtesy name Tingzhan, was registered in a civilian household in Guang’an Subprefecture, Shunqing Prefecture, Sichuan. A student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked fourth in his family and was aged thirty-three, born on the fifteenth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Xuan, his grandfather Ji, an Assistant Instructor, his father Boxiang, and his mother née Jin. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His elder brothers were Mian, an official awaiting selection for appointment, Guan, and Fu; his younger brothers were Kai, Qin, Zao, Hua, Fen, and Kui. He married a woman née Li. He placed fifty-third in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 127th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Ren, courtesy name Yuanfu, was registered in a civilian household in Dong’e County, Dongping Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong. A county school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked first in his family and was aged thirty-five, born on the seventh day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Sheng, his grandfather Xiang, his father Xuan, a Clerk, and his mother née Hu. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Lan, Zhen, a sacrificial official (shengji guan), and Shen; his younger brother was Fan. He married a woman née Liu. He placed first in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 105th in the Metropolitan Examination.

閻溥〔貫陝西西安府興平縣，民籍，國子生，治書經，字公甫，行四，年三十九，七月十三日生〕。曾祖通〔刑部司獄，贈順天府府尹〕，祖鐸〔順天府府尹〕，父璘〔鴻臚寺序班〕，母趙氏。永感下，兄江、瀚、滄、沭、淅，弟濟，娶王氏，繼娶王氏。陝西鄉試第四十六名，會試第三百六十七名。
translation_en:
Kang He 康河, courtesy name Deqing, was registered in Wugong County, Qian Subprefecture, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi, in a civilian household. A county government school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was twelfth in birth order, aged thirty-four, and born on the eighteenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather Jue was Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices in Nanjing; his grandfather Jian was Administrative Clerk in the Office of Transmission; and his father Luan was an honorary official, posthumously granted the title of Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue. His father’s former wife, née Gao, and his mother, née Gao, were both posthumously granted the title of Lady of Peace (anren). Both his parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Fu, Huai, Hong, Ze (Instructor of Medicine), Hai (formerly a Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy), Run, Hao (a Subprefect promoted to Director in the Ministry of Revenue), Han, Chun, and Yang (an honorary official); his younger brother was Lian. He married a woman née Duan. He placed thirteenth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 387th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yan Pu 閻溥, courtesy name Gongfu, was registered in Xingping County, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi, in a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, he was fourth in birth order, aged thirty-nine, and born on the thirteenth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather Tong was Prison Warden in the Ministry of Justice, posthumously granted the title of Prefect of Shuntian; his grandfather Duo was Prefect of Shuntian; and his father Lin was an Usher in the Court of State Ceremonial. His mother was née Zhao. Both his parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Jiang, Han, Cang, Shu, and Xi; his younger brother was Ji. He married a woman née Wang and subsequently married another woman née Wang. He placed forty-sixth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 367th in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
臣姚淶
臣對臣聞善治天下者固在乎立大法以為致
治之具尤貴乎端大本以為出治之要何謂大
法經綸政務之道康濟民物之方是也何謂大
本人主一心所以宰政務而御民物者是也無
是法則雖有願治之心而因革常患於失宜無
是心則雖有圖治之迹而先後常病於無序如
是而欲綱紀之正風俗之厚治功之善得乎故
心所以宰制乎法而法所以推行其心法者治
之具而心者治之要也得其要者固不可不求
===
其具得其具者尤不可不先其要古之善治天
下者無他焉亦惟循用此道而已矣後世之所
以不古若者豈非徒恃乎法制以為治具而未
能先正其本原以為治要歟欽惟
皇帝陛下以剛健純粹之資高明光大之學
入紹大統光濟前休啓中興之令圖開太平之昌
曆嘉靖天下以綱紀風俗為慮進臣等於
廷而
賜之清問所謂知出天下而聽於至愚威加四海
而屈於匹夫可與為堯舜可與為湯武者也顧

臣姚淶

臣對：臣聞善治天下者，固在乎立大法以為致治之具，尤貴乎端大本以為出治之要。何謂大法？經綸政務之道、康濟民物之方是也。何謂大本？人主一心所以宰政務而御民物者是也。無是法，則雖有願治之心，而因革常患於失宜；無是心，則雖有圖治之迹，而先後常病於無序。如是而欲綱紀之正、風俗之厚、治功之善，得乎？故心所以宰制乎法，而法所以推行其心。法者，治之具；而心者，治之要也。得其要者，固不可不求其具；得其具者，尤不可不先其要。古之善治天下者，無他焉，亦惟循用此道而已矣。後世之所以不古若者，豈非徒恃乎法制以為治具，而未能先正其本原以為治要歟？欽惟皇帝陛下，以剛健純粹之資、高明光大之學，入紹大統，光濟前休，啓中興之令圖，開太平之昌曆，嘉靖天下，以綱紀風俗為慮，進臣等於廷，而賜之清問。所謂知出天下而聽於至愚，威加四海而屈於匹夫，可與為堯舜，可與為湯武者也。顧
translation_en:
Your servant, Yao Lai 姚淶.

Your servant replies: I have heard that those who govern All under Heaven well must indeed establish great laws as the instruments for achieving good government, but above all must set right the great foundation as the essential source of government. What are the great laws? They are the principles for ordering affairs of state and the methods for bringing well-being and relief to the people and all things. What is the great foundation? It is the ruler’s own heart, by which he directs affairs of state and governs the people and all things. Without these laws, even with a heart desirous of good government, one constantly risks acting inappropriately in retaining or changing existing institutions. Without this heart, even with outward efforts toward good government, one constantly suffers from a lack of order in determining what should come first and what afterward. Under such conditions, can one hope for proper governing principles and discipline, sound customs, and successful government? Thus the heart directs and controls the laws, while the laws put the heart’s intentions into effect. Laws are the instruments of government; the heart is its essential element. Those who grasp the essential element must certainly seek its instruments; those who possess its instruments must above all give priority to its essential element. Those of antiquity who governed All under Heaven well had no other method: they simply followed and applied this Way. Is the reason later ages have fallen short of antiquity not that they have relied solely on laws and institutions as instruments of government, without first rectifying their source as the essential basis of government?

I reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor, endowed with strength, vigor, and purity, and with lofty, enlightened, broad, and luminous learning, has succeeded to the imperial line, splendidly carried forward the accomplishments of your predecessors, initiated an excellent plan for dynastic revival, and opened a flourishing era of great peace. You have brought good order and tranquility to All under Heaven, taking governing principles, discipline, and customs as your concerns. You have summoned us, your servants, to court and graciously bestowed upon us your discerning questions. This is what is meant by one whose wisdom surpasses all under Heaven yet listens to the most foolish, whose might extends throughout the Four Seas yet condescends to an ordinary man—one who can become a Yao or Shun, a Tang or Wu. Yet…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
以臣之謭陋不足以贊
廟謨裨國論然而一得之愚亦安敢不為
陛下効之乎臣惟人君膺天眷之隆為生民之主固
不能舎法以圖治亦不專恃法以為治盖四海
至廣兆民至衆苟無法以維持之則何以一其
心志而使之各循其理何以息其爭奪而使之
各安其分故自古帝王欲成天下之治必順時
揆事創制立法以盡天下之務而定為一代之
規如禮以正名分樂以格神人律以和聲曆以
授時疆理宇內以柔遠能邇設立庶官以代天
===
任事分田制賦以足國裕民興學養士以惇化
善俗選舉以興賢能考課以計吏治兵戎以禦
外侮刑罰以詰姦慝是皆治具之大所當修舉
焉者雖世有升降政有因革未有舎此而能圖
治者也然禮樂教化由心而發典章文物由心
而著家齊國治天下平由心而推人君一心寔
建立法制之本而推行之序必自此始焉先儒
朱熹嘗論善為治者必先有綱紀以持之於上
而後有風俗以驅之於下又謂綱紀不能以自
立必人主之心術公平正大無偏黨反側之私

而著家齊國治天下平由心而推人君一心寔
建立法制之本而推行之序必自此始焉先儒
朱熹嘗論善爲治者必先有綱紀以持之於上
而後有風俗以驅之於下又謂綱紀不能以自
立必人主之心術公平正大無偏黨反側之私
punctuated:
以臣之謭陋，不足以贊廟謨、裨國論，然而一得之愚，亦安敢不為陛下効之乎？臣惟人君膺天眷之隆，為生民之主，固不能舎法以圖治，亦不專恃法以為治。盖四海至廣，兆民至衆，苟無法以維持之，則何以一其心志而使之各循其理？何以息其爭奪而使之各安其分？故自古帝王欲成天下之治，必順時揆事，創制立法，以盡天下之務，而定為一代之規。如禮以正名分，樂以格神人，律以和聲，曆以授時，疆理宇內以柔遠能邇，設立庶官以代天任事，分田制賦以足國裕民，興學養士以惇化善俗，選舉以興賢能，考課以計吏治，兵戎以禦外侮，刑罰以詰姦慝，是皆治具之大，所當修舉焉者。雖世有升降，政有因革，未有舎此而能圖治者也。

然禮樂教化由心而發，典章文物由心而著，家齊國治天下平由心而推。人君一心，寔建立法制之本，而推行之序，必自此始焉。先儒朱熹嘗論，善為治者，必先有綱紀以持之於上，而後有風俗以驅之於下。又謂，綱紀不能以自立，必人主之心術公平正大，無偏黨反側之私
translation_en:
…with my shallow and limited understanding, I am unworthy to assist the deliberations of the throne or contribute to discussions of state affairs. Yet how could I dare withhold from Your Majesty even the single insight that a fool may gain? Your servant considers that the ruler, receiving Heaven’s abundant favor and serving as lord of the people, certainly cannot dispense with laws in seeking good government; neither can he rely exclusively on laws to govern. The lands within the Four Seas are exceedingly vast, and the people exceedingly numerous. Without laws to hold them together, how could their intentions be unified and each be made to follow proper principles? How could their contention and strife be stilled and each be made content with his allotted station? Thus, from antiquity, emperors and kings seeking to bring order to the world have invariably adapted to the times and weighed affairs, creating institutions and establishing laws to encompass all the world’s business and fix the governing standards of their dynasty. Ritual rectifies names and distinctions of status; music moves spirits and people; pitch standards harmonize sounds; the calendar makes the seasons known. Territorial boundaries and administration bring those far away into peaceful submission and foster concord with those nearby. The establishment of the various offices provides for carrying out affairs on Heaven’s behalf. The allocation of fields and regulation of taxation provide sufficient resources for the state and prosperity for the people. The founding of schools and nurturing of scholars strengthen moral instruction and improve customs. Selection and recommendation advance the worthy and capable; performance evaluations assess officials’ administration; military forces repel aggression from outside; punishments bring treachery and wrongdoing to account. These are all major instruments of government that ought to be maintained and put into effect. Though ages rise and decline, and policies are retained or altered, no one has ever been able to seek good government while abandoning these things.

Yet ritual, music, and moral instruction issue from the mind; institutions and the forms of civilization manifest themselves from the mind; the ordering of the family, the governing of the state, and the pacification of the world extend outward from the mind. The ruler’s mind is truly the foundation for establishing laws and institutions, and the sequence of putting them into practice must begin here. The earlier Confucian scholar Zhu Xi once argued that those skilled in governing must first have guiding principles and disciplinary order to uphold government above, and then customs to impel the people below. He also said that such order cannot establish itself: the ruler’s disposition and intentions must be impartial, fair, upright, and magnanimous, free from the selfishness of factional bias and deviousness…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
然後綱紀有所繫而立盖所謂綱紀者必辨賢
否以定上下之分核功罪以公賞罰之施所謂
風俗者必使人皆知善之可慕而必為皆知不
善之可羞而必去也君臣之間苟知轉移振舉
之機莫急於此宰執秉持而不敢失臺諫補察
而無所私人主又以其大公至正之心恭己於
上而照臨之則有所不為為之而無不成有所
不革革之而無不服將見法制以綱紀之立而
無頺墮廢墜之虞風俗以法制之行而無偷薄
頑獷之習本末兼舉上下相因而天下之治於
===
是乎成矣顧其張弛醇雜皆本於君心之能正
與否此則治要之大尤當致意焉者又豈專恃
乎法制哉臣伏讀
聖制盖已深察乎此臣請以經之所載為
陛下陳之夫禮樂之為用大矣在唐虞則巡狩以修
五禮典樂以諧八音在三代則大宗伯掌五禮
以防民偽大司樂掌六樂以防民情盖建諸天
地而同節同和者也律曆之所關重矣在唐虞
則在璣衡以齊七政考聲律以察治忽在三代
則五紀用序而時以定七音始備而聲以和盖

…only then do the guiding principles of government have an anchor and become established. These guiding principles require distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy to determine the distinctions between superior and subordinate, and assessing achievements and offenses to ensure impartial rewards and punishments. As for customs, everyone must be made to understand that goodness deserves admiration and must be practiced, and that wrongdoing deserves shame and must be abandoned. If ruler and ministers understand the means of bringing about change and renewal, nothing is more urgent than this. Let the chief councilors uphold these principles without daring to neglect them, and the censorial and remonstrance officials correct omissions and scrutinize affairs without partiality. Let the ruler, with a supremely impartial and upright mind, maintain a reverent bearing above and oversee them. Then, though there may be things he leaves undone, whatever he undertakes will succeed; though there may be things he leaves unchanged, whatever he reforms will command submission. We shall then see laws and institutions, sustained by established guiding principles, free from the danger of deterioration and abandonment, and customs, shaped by the implementation of those laws and institutions, free from habits of indifference, meanness, obstinacy, and unruliness. With both root and branches attended to, and those above and below supporting one another, orderly government throughout the realm will thus be achieved. Yet whether these principles are firmly maintained or slackened, and whether customs are pure or mixed, all depends on whether the ruler’s mind can be upright. This is a matter of the greatest importance among the essentials of government, deserving particular attention. How could one rely exclusively on laws and institutions?
Your servant has reverently read Your Majesty’s imperial pronouncement: you have already perceived this deeply. I beg to set forth for Your Majesty what is recorded in the Classics. Great indeed is the function of rites and music! In the time of Tang and Yu, inspection tours were conducted to put the five categories of rites in order, and the Director of Music harmonized the eight classes of musical sound. Under the Three Dynasties, the Minister of Rites administered the five categories of rites to guard against deceit among the people, and the Music Master administered the six musical performances to restrain the people’s passions. In the time of Tang and Yu, the astronomical instrument was examined [?] to bring the seven celestial regulators into accord, and sounds and pitch standards were investigated to discern good government or neglect. title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
協於陰陽而至精至密者也封山濬川而五服
之遠近規畫甚詳體國經野而九州之險易界
限不紊此其疆理宇內載諸禹貢職方者可述
也詢咨岳牧而又分命九官以時亮天工訓迪
公孤而又分命六卿以率屬倡牧此其設立庶
官載諸舜典周官者可稽也咸則三壤成賦中
邦此唐虞之田賦也夏貢殷助周則兼而用之
大學上庠小學下庠此唐虞之學校也夏校殷
序周則兼而舉之其選舉也翕受敷施九德咸
事在於唐虞者如此而夏官所謂以德詔爵以
===
功詔祿以能詔事以久奠食者亦三代之常制
也其考課也三載考績黜陟幽明在於唐虞者
如此而天官所謂宰夫受日考小宰受月考大
宰受歲考三歲則大計吏治而誅賞之者亦三
代之盛典也以言其兵比閭族黨即伍兩軍旅
之師蒐苗獮狩皆征伐擊刺之術茲非兵制之
善者乎以言乎刑皐陶為士能體夫欽恤之仁
吕刑有誥猶存夫敬慎之意又非刑罰之善者
乎斯蓋帝王之治法真足以為萬世之法程者
也然而數聖人者皆得夫建立之本而不紊於

translation_en:
…harmonizing with yin and yang with the utmost precision and exactitude. They marked out the mountains and dredged the rivers, planning in great detail the nearer and more distant zones of the five domains of service. They laid out the capitals and surveyed the countryside, keeping the boundaries of difficult and accessible terrain throughout the Nine Provinces in orderly distinction. Their delimitation and ordering of the realm, recorded in the “Tribute of Yu” and “Offices of the Regions,” can thus be recounted. They consulted the regional overseers and governors, and separately appointed the nine officials to assist Heaven’s work in due season. They instructed the Three Dukes and Three Solitaries, and separately appointed the six ministers to lead their subordinates and guide the governors. Their establishment of the various offices, recorded in the “Canon of Shun” and “Offices of Zhou,” can thus be examined.

All three classes of soil were taken as the standard for fixing the levies of the central lands: this was the land taxation of Tang and Yu. The Xia used the tribute system, the Yin the labor-assistance system, and the Zhou employed both. The greater school was the Upper Xiang, and the lesser school the Lower Xiang: these were the schools of Tang and Yu. The Xia had the jiao and the Yin the xu, and the Zhou maintained both. As for their selection and appointment of men, they received talent broadly and distributed appointments, so that men possessing the nine virtues all served: such was the practice under Tang and Yu. What the “Offices of Summer” describes—recommending rank according to virtue, emoluments according to achievement, duties according to ability, and fixing stipends according to length of service—was likewise the regular system of the Three Dynasties.

As for evaluating officials, their achievements were assessed every three years, and the unworthy were dismissed while the worthy were promoted: such was the practice under Tang and Yu. What the “Offices of Heaven” describes—the Assistant Administrator receiving daily assessments, the Vice Minister of State receiving monthly assessments, and the Minister of State receiving annual assessments, with a comprehensive review of officials’ administration every three years followed by punishments and rewards—was likewise a splendid institution of the Three Dynasties. To speak of their military arrangements, the residential groupings of bi, lü, zu, and dang constituted the troops organized into squads, platoons, armies, and battalions. The spring, summer, autumn, and winter hunts all provided training in campaigning, striking, and thrusting. Was this not an excellent military system? To speak of punishments, Gao Yao, as Minister of Justice, embodied the benevolence of reverent care and compassion. The proclamation in the “Punishments of Lü” likewise preserved this spirit of reverence and caution. Was this not also an excellent administration of punishment?

These were indeed the methods of government of the ancient emperors and kings, truly sufficient to serve as standards for all ages. Yet those several sages all grasped the foundation on which these institutions were established, and did not introduce disorder into…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
推行之序精一執中堯舜禹盖以心法而相授
是以任賢去邪罔惑於疑貳命德討罪允協於
明威其綱紀在上者無不張矣當是之時黎民
於變而萬邦咸寧臣庶協中而四方風動其致
雍熙泰和之盛豈不宜哉建中建極商湯周武
盖以心法而相傳是以懋官懋賞必論其功德
而私昵不得以苟容三宅三俊必任夫吉士而
憸人不得以相間其綱紀在上者無不張矣當
是之時商邑用協而四方見德時罔不變而允
升大猷其致雍熙泰和之盛豈不宜哉三代而
===
下雖有願治之君而於為治之法或未能畢舉
雖有為治之法而於出治之本或未能深探其
治之不古若有由然矣在漢則創業如高帝中
興如光武恭儉如孝文雄畧如孝武綜核如孝
宣明察如明寛厚如章皆一代之賢君也用叔
孫通之綿蕞歌唐山之樂章考落下閎之筭法
參司馬遷之律書建立郡國而統之以十三部
官分中外而列之以十六等輕徭薄賦而賜民
田租臨雍拜老而諸儒問難興廉舉孝則見於
元朔之詔考試功能則總於丞相之課郡國有

…the proper sequence of putting them into practice. Through refinement and single-mindedness, holding fast to the Mean, Yao, Shun, and Yu transmitted to one another the teaching of the mind. Thus they employed the worthy and removed the wicked, unconfused by doubt or divided counsels; they appointed the virtuous and punished the guilty, duly joining enlightened judgment with authority. The guiding principles of government were fully upheld above. At that time, the common people were transformed and the myriad states enjoyed peace; ministers and commoners conformed to the Mean, and the four quarters responded as grass bends before the wind. Was it not fitting that they should attain such flourishing concord and supreme harmony? By establishing the Mean and the supreme standard, Tang of Shang and King Wu of Zhou likewise transmitted the teaching of the mind. Thus, when generously granting offices and rewards, they invariably assessed merit and virtue, so that private favorites could not secure undeserved acceptance. For the three classes of office and their three classes of outstanding men, they invariably appointed good men, so that the unscrupulous could not intrude. The guiding principles of government were fully upheld above. At that time, the settlements of Shang were brought into concord, and the four quarters witnessed their virtue; none failed to be transformed, and all truly advanced along the great Way. Was it not fitting that they should attain such flourishing concord and supreme harmony?

After the Three Dynasties, although there were rulers who desired good government, they sometimes failed to implement all its methods; although methods of government existed, they sometimes failed to probe deeply into the root from which good government proceeds. There were therefore reasons why their government did not equal that of antiquity. In the Han, there were Gao Di, who founded the dynasty; Guangwu, who restored it; Xiaowen, reverent and frugal; Xiaowu, bold in strategic vision; Xiaoxuan, thorough in scrutiny; Ming, perceptive and discerning; and Zhang, generous and kind. All were worthy rulers of their age. They employed Shusun Tong’s ceremonial arrangements, marked out with cords and bundles of reeds; sang Tangshan’s musical hymns; examined Luoxia Hong’s calendrical calculations; and consulted Sima Qian’s Treatise on Pitch-Pipes. They established commanderies and kingdoms, coordinating them through thirteen regions; divided officials between the central and local administrations, arranging them in sixteen grades; reduced labor service and taxation, and granted the people remission of land taxes; and visited the Biyong academy to pay homage to the elders, while the Confucian scholars questioned and debated one another. title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
材官之設京師有南北之屯而内外足以相制
次律令以示畫一除肉刑以全民生而仁恩足
以勝殘其法制亦云備矣在唐則文武兼資有
如文皇初政勵精有如玄宗剛明果斷有如憲
宗皆一代之賢君也新禮修於房玄齡雅樂定
於祖孝孫清聲作於開元曆法備於大衍因山
川之形便而分道立州倣六卿之率屬而限官
任才口分世業而井田之制尚存大召名儒而
弘文之館肇立選人之途有四而主以三銓之
法考功之善有四而差以九等之制建府立衛
===
則似鄉遂之師矜刑慎獄則謹覆奏之令其法
制亦云備矣在宋則仁孝豁達有如藝祖克篤
前烈有如太宗忠厚惻怛有如仁宗皆一代之
賢君也有禮圖纂義諸書有平晉大安諸樂和
峴論鐘律而胡瑗范鎮之說迭興司天修曆法
而觀天統元之名繼作建官始於乾德而元豐
則又新之分路始於太宗而神宗則又增之履
畝制稅而限天下之田興學育材而崇蘇湖之
教踵唐規以銓試而益以律令經義之條設磨
勘以遞遷而主以審官考課之院設禁兵以備

…trained infantry were established, while the capital had its Southern and Northern garrisons, so that forces within and outside the capital could adequately check one another. Statutes and ordinances were arranged to establish uniform standards, and mutilating punishments were abolished to preserve the people's lives; benevolence and grace thus sufficed to overcome cruelty. Its laws and institutions, too, could be called comprehensive.
Under the Tang, there were rulers such as Emperor Wen, endowed with both civil and military abilities; Xuanzong, who applied himself vigorously to government early in his reign; and Xianzong, firm, discerning, and decisive. All were worthy rulers of their age. Fang Xuanling compiled new rites, and Zu Xiaosun established the ceremonial music. Pure musical tones were developed during the Kaiyuan era, and calendrical methods were perfected in the Dayan calendar. Circuits were divided and prefectures established according to the advantageous configuration of mountains and rivers. Following the model of the Six Ministers directing their subordinates, official posts were delimited and talented men appointed. With land allotted per person and land held hereditarily, something of the well-field system still survived. Eminent Confucian scholars were summoned in large numbers, and the Institute for the Advancement of Literature was first established. There were four routes for selecting men for office, governed principally by the procedures of the three selection authorities. There were four qualities of merit in evaluating performance, with distinctions made according to a system of nine grades. Establishing military headquarters and guards resembled the armies of the townships and outlying districts. Compassion in punishment and caution in adjudication were expressed through scrupulous observance of the rules for resubmitting cases to the throne for review. Its laws and institutions, too, could be called comprehensive.
Under the Song, there were rulers such as Yizu, humane, filial, and broad-minded; Taizong, who faithfully carried forward his predecessor's achievements; and Renzong, loyal, generous, compassionate, and solicitous. All were worthy rulers of their age. There were books such as Illustrations of Ritual (Litu) and Collected Interpretations (Zuanyi), and musical compositions such as Pacification of Jin (Ping Jin) and Great Peace (Da An). He Xian discussed bells and pitch standards, and the theories of Hu Yuan and Fan Zhen arose in succession. The astronomical authorities revised calendrical methods, and calendars bearing the names Observing Heaven (Guantian) and Unifying the Origin (Tongyuan) appeared one after another. The establishment of official posts began in the Qiande era, and in the Yuanfeng era the system was renewed. The division into circuits began under Taizong, and Shenzong further increased their number. Taxes were assessed by measuring fields, and limits were imposed on landholdings throughout the realm. Schools were promoted and talent cultivated, with esteem accorded to the teaching methods of Suzhou and Huzhou. 於天下置審刑院於禁中而刑獄不濫其法制
亦云備矣夫法制雖備而世主無正心之學不
悅詩書專尚黃老習于刑名惑于符讖而七制

夫法制雖備，而世主無正心之學，不悅詩書，專尚黃老，習于刑名，惑于符讖，而七制之心術已荒；首復浮屠，行瀆人倫，耽于聲色，溺于佛骨，而三宗之心術已壞；陳橋啓祚，金匱渝盟，或矯誣不明，或剛斷不足，而宋世人主之心術亦未有能自正者。是以當時之治，賞者未必有功，而罰者未必有罪；上者未必皆賢，而下者未必皆不肖。舉其大者言之，如疎賈誼而親鄧通，外汲黯而內平津，王吉謝病而恭顯用事，韓歆被譴而子密受封，漢之綱紀豈能盡正哉？信不能保魏徵之直，而許敬宗得以列于朝；明不能燭林甫之姦，而張九齡無以安其位；李絳與吐突承璀而並進，裴度與皇甫鎛而兼收，唐之綱紀豈能盡正哉？竇儼以宿儒受知，而盧多遜之憸邪則弗之覺；柴禹錫以上變見用，而王禹偁之抗言則弗之容；歐陽脩論朋黨而無補於去留，范仲淹抑僥倖而不勝其讒謗，宋之綱紀又豈能盡正哉？夫上下之分不定，而賞罰之施

…to guard the palace, and stationed prefectural troops under the various prefectures; thus the military organization, too, was carefully elaborated. Edicts enjoining compassion in punishment were promulgated throughout the empire, and a Court of Judicial Review was established within the palace precincts, preventing abuses in criminal proceedings. Its laws and institutions could indeed be called comprehensive.
Yet although laws and institutions were comprehensive, the rulers of those ages lacked the learning needed to rectify their minds. They took no delight in the Odes and Documents, exclusively esteemed the teachings of Huangdi and Laozi, were habituated to the techniques of punishments and administrative accountability, and were deluded by auspicious tokens and prophetic writings: thus the moral dispositions of the seven Han sovereigns had already fallen into neglect. Taking the lead in restoring Buddhism, acting in ways that defiled human relationships, indulging in music and sensual pleasures, and becoming infatuated with the Buddha’s bone: thus the moral dispositions of the three Tang emperors had already been corrupted. With the founding of the dynasty at Chenqiao and the violation of the covenant preserved in the golden coffer, there was either deception and a lack of clarity, or insufficient firmness and resolution. Among the rulers of the Song, too, none was able to rectify his own moral disposition. Consequently, under the governments of those times, those rewarded did not necessarily possess merit, and those punished were not necessarily guilty; those in high positions were not necessarily all worthy, and those in low positions were not necessarily all unworthy.
To cite the major examples: Jia Yi was kept at a distance while Deng Tong was favored; Ji An was excluded while the Marquis of Pingjin was admitted to the inner circle; Wang Ji pleaded illness and withdrew while Gong and Xian wielded power; Han Xin was condemned while Zimi received a noble title. How could the governing order of the Han have been wholly correct? The ruler’s trust could not safeguard the upright Wei Zheng, yet Xu Jingzong secured a place at court; the ruler’s discernment could not expose Linfu’s treachery, while Zhang Jiuling could not remain secure in office. Li Jiang and Tutu Chengcui were advanced together, and Pei Du and Huangfu Bo were both accepted into service. How could the governing order of the Tang have been wholly correct? Dou Yan gained recognition as a seasoned Confucian scholar, yet Lu Duoxun’s sinister wickedness went undetected. Chai Yuxi gained employment by reporting a plot, yet Wang Yucheng’s forthright remonstrance was not tolerated. Ouyang Xiu discussed political factions, but this did nothing to improve decisions about retaining or dismissing officials; Fan Zhongyan curbed the pursuit of unearned advancement, but could not withstand the resulting slander. How, then, could the governing order of the Song have been wholly correct? When distinctions between those above and those below are not settled, and the dispensing of rewards and punishments…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
未公則法制何自而立風俗何自而厚乎故西
漢之風俗雖曰以經術為尚然觀德色誶語之
策四方逆賊之奏則所謂薄惡者亦有之矣東
漢之風俗雖曰以節義為尚然觀朱穆崇厚之
說潛夫浮侈之篇則所謂澆靡者亦有之矣唐
人尚詞章此風俗之近浮者也觀正俗之諷與
獨行之傳而有以知唐世之多僻宋人尚理學
此風俗之近古者也觀明禁之文與憫俗之論
而有以知宋俗之不淳上無綱紀以持之下無
風俗以驅之故漢之治效蓄積歲增戶口蕃息
===
禁網疎闊刑罰大省可以言治矣而不免有雜
霸之弊唐之治效斗米三錢牛馬被野民物阜
繁四夷降附可以言治矣而不免有雜夷之弊
宋之治效刑以不殺為威財以不蓄為富兵以
不用為功人材以不作聰明為賢可以言治矣
而不免有武畧不競之弊失其本原而徒恃法
制果可以為治哉仰惟我
太祖高皇帝肇造區夏創建宏規
太宗文皇帝中靖家邦纘述大統
列聖相承益隆不替道配帝王而治超近古豈無道

未公，則法制何自而立，風俗何自而厚乎？故西漢之風俗，雖曰以經術為尚，然觀德色誶語之策、四方逆賊之奏，則所謂薄惡者亦有之矣。東漢之風俗，雖曰以節義為尚，然觀朱穆崇厚之說、《潛夫》浮侈之篇，則所謂澆靡者亦有之矣。唐人尚詞章，此風俗之近浮者也；觀正俗之諷與獨行之傳，而有以知唐世之多僻。宋人尚理學，此風俗之近古者也；觀明禁之文與憫俗之論，而有以知宋俗之不淳。上無綱紀以持之，下無風俗以驅之，故漢之治效，蓄積歲增，戶口蕃息，禁網疎闊，刑罰大省，可以言治矣，而不免有雜霸之弊。唐之治效，斗米三錢，牛馬被野，民物阜繁，四夷降附，可以言治矣，而不免有雜夷之弊。宋之治效，刑以不殺為威，財以不蓄為富，兵以不用為功，人材以不作聰明為賢，可以言治矣，而不免有武畧不競之弊。失其本原而徒恃法制，果可以為治哉？

仰惟我太祖高皇帝肇造區夏，創建宏規；太宗文皇帝中靖家邦，纘述大統；列聖相承，益隆不替。道配帝王，而治超近古，豈無道
translation_en:
…are not impartial, then how can laws and institutions be established, and how can customs become sound? Thus, although the Western Han is said to have esteemed classical learning, when we examine the policy essay concerning self-satisfied looks and abusive speech and the memorial concerning rebels throughout the realm, we find that what are called mean and wicked customs also existed. Although the Eastern Han is said to have esteemed integrity and righteousness, when we examine Zhu Mu’s discussion of fostering substantial virtue and the chapter on frivolous extravagance in Discourses of a Recluse (Qianfu), we find that what are called shallow and decadent customs also existed. The people of the Tang esteemed literary composition: in this their customs approached frivolity. From the admonition on rectifying customs and the biographies of men of singular conduct, we can see how many aberrations there were in the Tang age. The people of the Song esteemed the Learning of Principle: in this their customs approached those of antiquity. Yet from the text on clarifying prohibitions and the discourse lamenting customs, we can see that Song customs were not pure.

Above, there were no governing principles to sustain order; below, there were no sound customs to guide the people. Thus, among the achievements of Han government, reserves increased annually, the population multiplied, the net of prohibitions was loose, and punishments were greatly reduced. This may be called good government, yet it could not escape the fault of mixing in the methods of the hegemon. Among the achievements of Tang government, a dou of rice cost three cash, cattle and horses covered the fields, the people and their goods flourished in abundance, and the barbarians of the four quarters submitted and pledged allegiance. This may be called good government, yet it could not escape the fault of mixing in barbarian ways. Among the achievements of Song government, punishment derived its awe from refraining from execution; finance counted the absence of hoarding as wealth; military affairs counted not employing troops as success; and men of talent were considered worthy for not displaying cleverness. This may be called good government, yet it could not escape the fault of weakness in military strategy. If one loses the fundamental source and relies merely on laws and institutions, can one really govern well?

I reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao founded the realm of China and established its grand design; Emperor Taizong Wen restored peace within the ruling house and the state and carried forward the great imperial succession; and the succession of sage sovereigns increased its glory without decline. Their Way matched that of the ancient emperors and kings, and their government surpassed that of more recent ages. Could there have been no Way…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
以致之哉臣嘗莊誦
太祖高皇帝之聖訓矣如曰人主一心治化之本存
於中者無堯舜之心欲施於政者有堯舜之治
決不可得也又曰法度縱弛當在更張使紀綱
正而條目舉其要在明禮義正人心厚風俗以
為之本大哉
王言一哉
王心而又持之以敬
天愛民之誠勵之以求賢勤政之志究心於洪範之
學垂情於衍義之書故能潤色鴻業損益百王
===
如命牛諒制禮命陶凱定樂而中和之用著正
胡元之聲頒大統之曆而陰陽之候調內設京
畿外列藩省而疆理有方首明職掌次辨禮儀
而官規有叙差土田之高下以定賦稅而酌輕
重之宜立府縣之學校以明彝倫而廣絃誦之
化以經術取士而選舉精以年資叙遷而考課
實以五府治軍而總於本兵則兵政有統以六
律論刑而參以
大誥則吏治不苛信所謂端其大本而立其大法矣
則其復古帝王之治而陋漢唐宋於下風者端

punctuated:
以致之哉？臣嘗莊誦太祖高皇帝之聖訓矣。如曰：「人主一心，治化之本。存於中者無堯舜之心，欲施於政者有堯舜之治，決不可得也。」又曰：「法度縱弛，當在更張，使紀綱正而條目舉。其要在明禮義、正人心、厚風俗，以為之本。」大哉，王言！一哉，王心！而又持之以敬天愛民之誠，勵之以求賢勤政之志，究心於洪範之學，垂情於衍義之書，故能潤色鴻業，損益百王。
如命牛諒制禮，命陶凱定樂，而中和之用著；正胡元之聲，頒大統之曆，而陰陽之候調；內設京畿，外列藩省，而疆理有方；首明職掌，次辨禮儀，而官規有叙；差土田之高下以定賦稅，而酌輕重之宜；立府縣之學校以明彝倫，而廣絃誦之化；以經術取士，而選舉精；以年資叙遷，而考課實；以五府治軍，而總於本兵，則兵政有統；以六律論刑，而參以大誥，則吏治不苛。信所謂端其大本而立其大法矣。則其復古帝王之治而陋漢唐宋於下風者，端
translation_en:
…by which this was achieved? Your servant has reverently recited the sacred instructions of Emperor Taizu Gao. For example, he said: “The ruler’s heart alone is the foundation of governance and moral transformation. If what he harbors within is not the heart of Yao and Shun, yet he wishes his administration to achieve the governance of Yao and Shun, this is utterly impossible.” He also said: “When laws and institutions have grown lax, they must be reformed, so that the guiding principles are rectified and the detailed provisions put into effect. The essential thing is to clarify ritual propriety and righteousness, rectify people’s hearts, and enrich their customs, making these the foundation.” Great indeed were these royal words! Undivided indeed was the royal heart! He further sustained this with sincere reverence for Heaven and love for the people, and spurred himself on with the resolve to seek worthy men and attend diligently to government. He devoted his mind to the teachings of the Great Plan (Hongfan) and his attention to the Extended Meaning (Yanyi). Thus he could embellish his grand achievement and adapt the institutions of the kings of successive ages.
For example, he ordered Niu Liang to establish rites and Tao Kai to regulate music, making manifest the effects of equilibrium and harmony. He corrected the “sounds” of the non-Han Yuan dynasty [?] and promulgated the Grand Concordance Calendar (Datong), bringing the seasonal indications of yin and yang into accord. He established the capital region within and arranged the provinces beyond it, providing an orderly system of territorial administration. He first clarified official duties and then distinguished ritual procedures, giving order to official regulations. He graded farmland as higher or lower to determine taxation, weighing the appropriate balance between lighter and heavier burdens. He established schools in prefectures and counties to elucidate the constant human relationships, extending the civilizing influence of music and recitation. He recruited officials through their mastery of the Classics, making selection discerning; he ordered promotion by seniority, making performance evaluation substantive. He administered the armies through the Five Chief Military Commissions, with overall control vested in the Minister of War, thus unifying military administration. He determined punishments according to the “six statutes” [?], consulting also the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao), so that official administration was not harsh. Truly, this was what is meant by rectifying the great foundation and establishing the great laws. That he restored the governance of the ancient emperors and kings, leaving the Han, Tang, and Song far inferior, surely …

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
有自哉是以綱紀正而風俗厚法制舉而治化
隆百五十餘年于茲然成者易毁盈者必溢加
以正德以来權姦蠱惑而法令滋章
陛下應期而興適承其後此正
社稷安危之機生民休戚之端君子小人進退消長
之際天命人心去就離合之時臣謂
聖祖在天之靈不能無望於
陛下之大有為也昔者
踐祚之初
改元一詔萬化俱新如徵耆舊以表名德登才俊
===
以興事功容直諫以開言路斥佞倖以敦士習
誅姦逆以昭邦憲褒忠直以勵世風蠲逋負以
甦疲療洗煩苛以釋冤滯剔蠹弊以儲貨財清
冒濫以惜名器滌瑕以德消沴以和改紀其政
而綱紀振于上申訓其人而風俗移于下由是
海隅蒼生莫不翹首以望太平傾心以觀至化
正如天地久否忽泰則平日月久晦忽開則明
雷霆久蟄忽震則驚雲霧久鬱忽廓則清豈非
臣民之一快哉以
陛下功烈之盛化理之隆雖商宗周宣何以遠過然

punctuated:
有自哉！是以綱紀正而風俗厚，法制舉而治化隆，百五十餘年于茲。然成者易毁，盈者必溢，加以正德以来，權姦蠱惑而法令滋章。陛下應期而興，適承其後，此正社稷安危之機，生民休戚之端，君子小人進退消長之際，天命人心去就離合之時。臣謂聖祖在天之靈，不能無望於陛下之大有為也。
昔者踐祚之初，改元一詔，萬化俱新。如徵耆舊以表名德，登才俊以興事功，容直諫以開言路，斥佞倖以敦士習，誅姦逆以昭邦憲，褒忠直以勵世風，蠲逋負以甦疲療，洗煩苛以釋冤滯，剔蠹弊以儲貨財，清冒濫以惜名器，滌瑕以德，消沴以和，改紀其政而綱紀振于上，申訓其人而風俗移于下。由是海隅蒼生，莫不翹首以望太平，傾心以觀至化。正如天地久否，忽泰則平；日月久晦，忽開則明；雷霆久蟄，忽震則驚；雲霧久鬱，忽廓則清。豈非臣民之一快哉！以陛下功烈之盛，化理之隆，雖商宗周宣，何以遠過？然
translation_en:
…indeed had its source! Thus the guiding principles of government were set right and customs grew sound; laws and institutions were put into effect and civilizing government flourished. More than a hundred and fifty years have now passed. Yet what has been achieved is easily destroyed, and what is full must overflow. Moreover, since the Zhengde reign, powerful, treacherous ministers have beguiled and misled, while laws and ordinances have proliferated. Your Majesty arose in response to the appointed time and inherited precisely this aftermath. This is the critical juncture determining the security or peril of the altars of soil and grain, the starting point of the people's well-being or suffering, the moment when gentlemen and petty men advance or retreat, decline or flourish, and the time when Heaven's mandate and the people's allegiance depart or remain, separate or unite. Your servant believes that the spirit of the sagely founding ancestor in Heaven cannot but look to Your Majesty for great achievements.
At the beginning of Your Majesty's accession, a single edict changing the reign title renewed every aspect of governance. You summoned venerable elders to honor renowned virtue, promoted talented men to advance public achievements, welcomed forthright remonstrance to open channels of counsel, and dismissed flattering favorites to strengthen the conduct of scholars. You executed traitors and rebels to make manifest the laws of the realm, commended the loyal and upright to encourage good customs, remitted arrears to revive the exhausted [?], swept away vexatious and harsh measures to release those unjustly detained, eliminated corrupt abuses to build up material resources, and purged fraudulent and indiscriminate appointments to safeguard official titles and insignia. Through virtue you cleansed blemishes; through harmony you dispelled malign influences. You reordered government, restoring discipline above, and renewed instruction of the people, transforming customs below. Consequently, the common people even in the remotest coastal lands all lifted their heads in expectation of great peace and turned their hearts toward the prospect of consummate civilizing rule. It was just as when Heaven and Earth, long obstructed, suddenly attain harmonious intercourse and become tranquil; when the sun and moon, long obscured, suddenly emerge and shine brightly; when thunder, long dormant, suddenly resounds and startles; or when clouds and mist, long gathered, suddenly disperse and leave the sky clear. Was this not a great joy for your subjects? Given the splendor of Your Majesty's achievements and the flourishing of your civilizing government, how could even Gaozong of Shang and King Xuan of Zhou far surpass you? Yet…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
邊陲戒嚴而盜賊竊發乾象失度而災異頻仍
績效未臻和氣未應信有如
陛下所慮者雖修省之詔屢下而消弭之效未聞
陛下豈得晏然而已乎臣愚以為事必稽古所以立
法也所謂禮樂律曆之類皆法之所寓也
陛下誠能以稽古為務遠宗帝王近法
祖宗則典章經制因革適宜大法可立而治具彰矣
治必端本所以正心也所謂綱紀風俗之施皆
心之所推也
陛下誠能以端本為先委政大臣聽用臺諫則綱紀
===
風俗先後有序大本既端而治要舉矣夫如是
則大化神明而鴻恩博洽績效何患於弗臻日
月貞明而雨暘時若和氣何患於弗應
陛下求治之心不至是而有慰者乎抑臣猶有說焉
盖天下之治統於人主之心而人主之心天下
之所共賴者也心存於正則事無不正而天下
蒙其福心蔽於邪則事無不邪而天下與其憂
陛下知所以正心矣臣特慮夫操存之甚難而察識
之未至耳何者一心之微攻之者衆大官備玉
食之奉九御儼紫庭之列繁聲或是以悅耳采

punctuated:
邊陲戒嚴，而盜賊竊發；乾象失度，而災異頻仍。績效未臻，和氣未應，信有如陛下所慮者。雖修省之詔屢下，而消弭之效未聞，陛下豈得晏然而已乎？臣愚以為，事必稽古，所以立法也。所謂禮樂律曆之類，皆法之所寓也。陛下誠能以稽古為務，遠宗帝王，近法祖宗，則典章經制，因革適宜，大法可立而治具彰矣。治必端本，所以正心也。所謂綱紀風俗之施，皆心之所推也。陛下誠能以端本為先，委政大臣，聽用臺諫，則綱紀風俗，先後有序，大本既端而治要舉矣。夫如是，則大化神明而鴻恩博洽，績效何患於弗臻？日月貞明而雨暘時若，和氣何患於弗應？陛下求治之心，不至是而有慰者乎？

抑臣猶有說焉。盖天下之治，統於人主之心，而人主之心，天下之所共賴者也。心存於正，則事無不正，而天下蒙其福；心蔽於邪，則事無不邪，而天下與其憂。陛下知所以正心矣，臣特慮夫操存之甚難，而察識之未至耳。何者？一心之微，攻之者衆。大官備玉食之奉，九御儼紫庭之列，繁聲或是以悅耳，采
translation_en:
…the frontiers are on alert, yet bandits rise unexpectedly; celestial phenomena depart from their proper courses, and calamities and anomalies recur frequently. Results have yet to be achieved, and harmonious cosmic influences have yet to respond: matters are indeed as Your Majesty fears. Although edicts calling for self-cultivation and self-examination have repeatedly been issued, no success in dispelling these troubles has been reported. How, then, could Your Majesty simply remain at ease? In my humble view, affairs must be examined in light of antiquity, for this is the means of establishing institutions. Such matters as rites, music, pitch standards, and calendrical reckoning all embody institutional principles. If Your Majesty can truly make the study of antiquity your task, taking the ancient emperors and kings as your distant models and your imperial ancestors as your nearer models, then the preservation or alteration of statutes, regulations, and established institutions will be appropriate. The great guiding principles can be established, and the instruments of government made manifest. Government must rectify its root, for this is the means of rectifying the mind. The ordering of governing norms and popular customs is entirely an extension of the mind. If Your Majesty can truly give priority to rectifying the root, entrust government to the great ministers, and heed and employ the censors and remonstrance officials, then governing norms and popular customs will be addressed in their proper sequence. Once the great root is rectified, the essentials of government will be put into effect. In this way, your transforming influence will be wondrously efficacious and your abundant grace will reach everywhere: why worry that results will not be achieved? The sun and moon will shine steadily, and rain and sunshine will come in their proper seasons: why worry that harmonious cosmic influences will not respond? Could Your Majesty’s desire for good government find satisfaction before this is achieved?

Yet your servant still has something to say. The government of all under Heaven is unified in the ruler’s mind, and that mind is what all under Heaven depend upon. If the mind abides in rectitude, nothing done will fail to be upright, and all under Heaven will receive its blessings. If the mind is obscured by perversity, nothing done will be free of perversity, and all under Heaven will share its troubles. Your Majesty knows how to rectify the mind. My particular concern is only that holding fast to and preserving it is exceedingly difficult, and that discerning awareness may not yet be complete. Why is this? translation_en:
…colors may suffice to delight the eyes; favorites may anticipate your wishes and flatter you; wicked, self-serving influences may exploit an opening and gradually seep in. Treasuring a single object from afar may open the door to tribute offerings; indulging in one small amusement may begin a course of pleasure excursions. Rising late one morning may foster a gradual slide into idle ease; readily believing one remark may provide an opening for slanderers and flatterers. Giving free rein to gratification in one affair is how commands come to be issued lightly; granting one favor indiscriminately is how hopes of undeserved advancement are encouraged. All these things can harm good government. Should you be even slightly beguiled by them, I fear that Your Majesty’s mind may no longer retain its former openness, clarity, stillness, and singleness of purpose. I wish Your Majesty to guard against them and proceed cautiously, reflecting deeply on the lessons of past events and making lasting plans to persevere to the end.

Nurture the beginnings of goodness and cultivate the root of good government. In private solitude, where you could act without restraint, you must exercise strict self-control; amid the buffeting waves of splendor and luxury, you must remain firmly composed. You must vigorously correct feelings of love and hatred that you might readily indulge, and guard deeply against sweet and pleasing words. Regard the teachings of the sages as what you ought to follow, and the government of the former kings as worthy of emulation. Gather the wisdom of all under Heaven to assist your discernment, so that nothing obstructs your sight or hearing; accord with the hearts of all under Heaven in issuing commands, so that no partiality governs what you accept or reject. Morning and evening, even in dreams, bear concern for the common people within the Four Seas. Laboring at affairs late into the night and from before dawn, keep in mind the enduring welfare of the ancestral temples and altars of state for ten thousand years.

If you do this, the mind that is the source of all will grow clearer each day. Thus you will seek the achievements of emperors and kings through their Way, and preserve the enterprise of your imperial ancestors through their institutions. The guiding principles of government will always be maintained and never slacken; customs will always remain generous and never become mean; the great laws…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
臣王教
臣對臣聞帝王致天下之治者其大有三大法
也大本也大幾也夫規制畫一條約詳明凡所
以予奪而為榮辱黜陟而為勸懲皆法也然惟
關天下是非之同繫人心可否之當上不失先
王之成憲下可為後世之永式循之則治隆而
俗美違之則教弛而風漓斯則謂之大法感而
遂通觸焉即應凡所以主張乎庶物綱維乎眾
事皆本也然惟至公足以絶天下之私至正足
以杜天下之邪取之不窮用之不竭百慮一致
===
而即此以生一日萬幾而胥此以應斯則謂之
大本理之將窮損益以出數之將終因革以異
凡所以可趨而謂之時可乗而謂之勢皆幾也
然惟中其會則逸而有成失其便則勞而無功
來不可禦於倏忽之間去不可追於猶豫之後
繫國家之安危關天下之理亂斯則謂之大幾
夫法者治之具也本者法之源也幾者事之會
也非大本之立固無以致大法之行若大幾有
不能决則必先其所後後其所先因其所革革
其所因所謂機會一失噬臍無及雖有其大法

punctuated:
臣王教。

臣對：臣聞帝王致天下之治者，其大有三：大法也，大本也，大幾也。夫規制畫一，條約詳明，凡所以予奪而為榮辱、黜陟而為勸懲，皆法也。然惟關天下是非之同，繫人心可否之當，上不失先王之成憲，下可為後世之永式，循之則治隆而俗美，違之則教弛而風漓，斯則謂之大法。感而遂通，觸焉即應，凡所以主張乎庶物、綱維乎眾事，皆本也。然惟至公足以絶天下之私，至正足以杜天下之邪，取之不窮，用之不竭，百慮一致而即此以生，一日萬幾而胥此以應，斯則謂之大本。理之將窮，損益以出；數之將終，因革以異。凡所以可趨而謂之時、可乗而謂之勢，皆幾也。然惟中其會則逸而有成，失其便則勞而無功，來不可禦於倏忽之間，去不可追於猶豫之後，繫國家之安危，關天下之理亂，斯則謂之大幾。夫法者，治之具也；本者，法之源也；幾者，事之會也。非大本之立，固無以致大法之行。若大幾有不能决，則必先其所後，後其所先，因其所革，革其所因。所謂機會一失，噬臍無及，雖有其大法
translation_en:
Your servant, Wang Jiao.

Your servant replies: I have heard that there are three great essentials by which emperors and kings bring good government to the realm: the great standards, the great foundation, and the great critical junctures. Uniform regulations and clearly detailed provisions—all the means by which granting and withholding confer honor and disgrace, and dismissal and promotion provide encouragement and chastisement—are standards. Yet only those that embody the realm’s shared judgment of right and wrong and accord with proper human judgments of approval and disapproval, that preserve the established institutions of the former kings and can serve as enduring models for later generations, merit the name “great standards.” Following them brings flourishing government and fine customs; departing from them brings lax moral instruction and deteriorating mores. That which, when stimulated, comprehends fully and, when touched, responds immediately—all that governs the myriad things and holds affairs together—is a foundation. Yet only that whose perfect impartiality suffices to eliminate all selfishness in the realm, and whose perfect rectitude suffices to prevent all perversity in the realm, merits the name “great foundation.” It can be drawn upon without exhaustion and used without depletion; the hundred deliberations converge upon a single end and arise from it, and the myriad affairs of each day are all answered through it. When an ordering principle is about to reach its limits, subtraction and addition open a way forward; when a cycle is about to end, continuity and change produce a different configuration. Everything that may be pursued as a timely opportunity or exploited as a prevailing configuration of circumstances constitutes a critical juncture. Yet only those junctures whose proper moment, if grasped, yields success with ease, but whose opportunity, if missed, yields toil without achievement, merit the name “great critical junctures.” Their sudden arrival cannot be checked, nor, once they have passed amid hesitation, can they be recalled; upon them depend the security or peril of the state and the order or disorder of the realm. Standards are the instruments of government; the foundation is the source of standards; critical junctures are the points at which affairs converge. Without establishing the great foundation, there is certainly no means of putting the great standards into practice. If one cannot reach a decision at a great critical juncture, one will inevitably put first what should come later and put later what should come first, preserve what should be changed and change what should be preserved. As the saying goes, once an opportunity is lost, biting one’s own navel in regret is of no avail. Even if one possesses the great standards…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
而掣肘難行矣臣嘗稽諸往牒惟二帝三王為
能全盡於此故其功德兼隆巍乎與天地同符
兩漢唐宋諸君率皆偏駁而不全故不能一一
以致其盛欽惟
皇帝陛下秉天地之全德撫盈成之景運懋修新政
率由舊章一予一奪一黜一陟罔不協于至公
合乎物議是天下有休寧之基而
宗社有靈長之慶可謂大法行矣然又從善如轉丸
決策如應響損益必中其會因革必就其便是
轉危而足以就安易亂而足以為治可謂大幾
===
決矣行是法也決是幾也皆
睿見之炳於先物
乾剛之執於獨斷浮議有不能惑羣邪有不能誘
純王之心布而為純王之政大本有弗立耶既
聖而不自聖已安而若未安乃於
萬幾之暇進臣等於
庭而策問之伏念愚臣草茅賤士章句腐儒當
龍飛取士之首科濫鴻漸于逵之末選自知迂疎
之論不足少裨於萬一然而際遇若此豈敢隱
默而不言哉臣惟天下之患嘗坐於委靡不振

punctuated:
而掣肘難行矣。臣嘗稽諸往牒，惟二帝三王為能全盡於此，故其功德兼隆，巍乎與天地同符。兩漢唐宋諸君，率皆偏駁而不全，故不能一一以致其盛。
欽惟皇帝陛下秉天地之全德，撫盈成之景運，懋修新政，率由舊章。一予一奪，一黜一陟，罔不協于至公，合乎物議。是天下有休寧之基，而宗社有靈長之慶，可謂大法行矣。然又從善如轉丸，決策如應響，損益必中其會，因革必就其便。是轉危而足以就安，易亂而足以為治，可謂大幾決矣。行是法也，決是幾也，皆睿見之炳於先物，乾剛之執於獨斷，浮議有不能惑，羣邪有不能誘。純王之心，布而為純王之政，大本有弗立耶？
既聖而不自聖，已安而若未安，乃於萬幾之暇，進臣等於庭而策問之。伏念愚臣，草茅賤士，章句腐儒，當龍飛取士之首科，濫鴻漸于逵之末選。自知迂疎之論，不足少裨於萬一，然而際遇若此，豈敢隱默而不言哉？臣惟天下之患，嘗坐於委靡不振。
translation_en:
…yet their implementation would be hampered and difficult. Your servant has examined the records of the past: only the Two Emperors and Three Kings were able to fulfill all these requirements completely. Thus their achievements and virtue alike flourished, towering in accord with Heaven and Earth. The rulers of the two Han dynasties, the Tang, and the Song were generally partial and inconsistent, lacking completeness; hence they could not each attain such flourishing greatness.
Reverently I consider that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses the complete virtue of Heaven and Earth and presides over an auspicious age of fullness and accomplishment. You diligently put new policies into practice while following established precedents. Every grant and withdrawal, every dismissal and promotion, accords with the utmost impartiality and conforms to public judgment. Thus All-under-Heaven has a foundation for peace and repose, and the imperial ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain enjoy the blessing of enduring perpetuity. We may say that the great laws are being implemented. Moreover, you follow what is good as readily as a ball rolls and decide policy as promptly as an echo responds. Your reductions and additions invariably meet the proper occasion, and your decisions to retain or reform invariably suit the circumstances. Thus you can turn danger into security and disorder into good government. We may say that the great critical junctures have been decisively addressed. The implementation of these laws and the resolution of these critical junctures alike arise from your sagacious insight, which shines forth before events unfold, and from your Heaven-like firmness, maintained in independent decision. Idle opinions cannot confuse you, nor can the host of the wicked entice you. A mind devoted purely to true kingship unfolds into a government devoted purely to true kingship. Could the great foundation fail to be established?
Already sagely, you do not regard yourself as a sage; already secure, you act as though security had yet to be attained. Thus, in an interval amid your myriad affairs of state, you brought us, your servants, before the court and questioned us on policy. Humbly I reflect that I, your ignorant servant, am a lowly scholar from the countryside, a pedantic Confucian confined to textual phrases and sentences. At this first examination for selecting scholars since your accession, I have undeservedly gained a place among the last selected to rise, like the wild goose, to the heights. I know that my impractical and ill-informed arguments cannot offer even the slightest assistance. Yet, having met with such an opportunity, how could I dare remain silent and withhold my words? Your servant considers that the troubles of All-under-Heaven have often arisen from listlessness and failure to rouse oneself…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
而奮發有為者獨能收致治之成功何哉為其
振綱紀於上美風俗於下也綱紀不振則政必
玩玩則弛弛則至於不可收拾而天下風俗隨
之矣故綱紀之振者必有以致風俗之美風俗
之美未嘗不本於綱紀之振自古帝王之順時
揆事創制立法一皆由斯道也帝之聖者莫如
堯舜王之聖者莫如禹湯文武其在當時黎民
敏德萬國咸寧人人有君子之行比屋有可封
之俗五刑措而不用兵革櫜而不試山川鬼神
無乎不寧鳥獸魚鱉罔不咸若其致雍熈泰和
===
之盛卓然為萬世之法程信如
聖制之所諭也要其大法之立有禮以别上下而冠
婚喪祭朝覲會同以至射飲食饗之有節有樂
以和神人而大章大韶大夏大濩以至大武諸
音之克和則禮樂定矣有律以求聲氣而權衡
輕重斗斛多寡丈尺長短以分有曆以紀歲時
而日月出沒寒暑往來人事興作以具則律曆
明矣體國經野畫土分域有以疆理宇内而為
九州十二州千里百里七十五十里之制經邦

之盛卓然為萬世之法程信如
聖制之所諭也要其大法之立有禮以別上下而冠
婚喪祭朝覲會同以至射飲食饗之有節有樂
以和神人而大章大韶大夏大濩以至大武諸
音之克和則禮樂定矣有律以求聲氣而權衡
輕重斗斛多寡丈尺長短以分有曆以紀歲時
而日月出沒寒暑往來人事興作以具則律曆
明矣體國經野畫土分域有以疆理宇內而為

translation_en:
…Yet those who rouse themselves to purposeful action alone succeed in bringing about good government. Why is this? Because they strengthen the governing framework above and improve customs below. If that framework is not strengthened, government inevitably becomes negligent; negligence leads to laxity, and laxity reaches the point where affairs can no longer be set right. The customs of the realm follow suit. Thus, strengthening the governing framework necessarily provides the means to improve customs; the excellence of customs has always been rooted in the strength of that framework. From antiquity, emperors and kings have followed this same way in responding to the times, assessing affairs, creating institutions, and establishing laws. Among the sage emperors, none surpassed Yao and Shun; among the sage kings, none surpassed Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu. In their time, the common people diligently pursued virtue, and the myriad states were all at peace. Everyone conducted himself as a gentleman, and customs were such that every household had people worthy of receiving a fief. The five punishments were laid aside unused, and weapons and armor were stored away without being put to the test. The spirits of mountains and rivers were all at peace, and birds, beasts, fish, and turtles all flourished in their proper order. The flourishing concord and supreme harmony they achieved stood forth as a model for all ages, just as Your Majesty’s decree has indeed declared.

To summarize the establishment of their fundamental institutions: there were rites to distinguish higher from lower, regulating capping, marriage, mourning, sacrifice, court audiences, and assemblies of rulers, as well as archery, ceremonial drinking, meals, and feasts. There was music to bring spirits and humans into harmony: the Great Manifestation (Dazhang), Great Succession (Dashao), Great Xia (Daxia), Great Protection (Dahuo), and Great Martial Dance (Dawu), whose various tones were all harmonious. Thus ritual and music were established. There were pitch standards for investigating sounds and vital energies, through which distinctions were made between heavier and lighter weights on balances, larger and smaller quantities measured in dou and hu, and longer and shorter lengths measured in zhang and chi. There was a calendar to record the years and seasons, fully accounting for the rising and setting of the sun and moon, the alternation of cold and heat, and the commencement of human activities. Thus pitch standards and calendrical reckoning were made clear. They laid out the capital and ordered the countryside, demarcated lands and divided territories, thereby establishing boundaries throughout the realm and creating the systems of nine provinces and twelve provinces, and of domains measuring one thousand, one hundred, seventy, and fifty li. They administered the realm and spread moral transformation, directed subordinates and apportioned duties, thereby establishing the various offices, including the Chief Minister and the Four Marchmounts…

維百維倍三百六十之員分田以給野人而制
賦以養君子有貢也助也徹也以至圭田五十
畝餘夫二十五畝其綜理之何其周興學以明
教而養士以儲材有校也序也庠也以至左學
右學虞庠國學其制度亦無不至自里選鄉舉
而至於王國則有造士進士由宗伯司馬以達
於王焉自翕受敷施而官於王朝則有三載考
績三考黜陟幽明焉因井制兵而寓兵於農無
事則執耒之夫有事則荷戈之卒也何有於不
掉之患乎刑故宥過而期於無刑五刑之屬若
===
嚴五用之法則恕也何有於禁網之密乎是即
臣所謂大法之立而為綱紀之振如此其致雍
熙泰和之盛而為風俗之美也宜哉雖然此特
其致治之具耳原其建立之本堯則克明峻德
也舜則允迪厥德也禹則祗台德先也湯則懋
昭大德建中於民也文武則緝熙敬止建其有
極也孰有外於此身此心者乎溯其推行之序
則自身以及於家為敦叙九族克諧以孝時庸
展親刑于寡妻也自家以及於國為平章百姓

維百維倍三百六十之員。分田以給野人，而制賦以養君子，有貢也、助也、徹也，以至圭田五十畝、餘夫二十五畝，其綜理之何其周！興學以明教，而養士以儲材，有校也、序也、庠也，以至左學、右學、虞庠、國學，其制度亦無不至。自里選鄉舉而至於王國，則有造士、進士，由宗伯、司馬以達於王焉。自翕受敷施而官於王朝，則有三載考績、三考黜陟幽明焉。因井制兵，而寓兵於農，無事則執耒之夫，有事則荷戈之卒也，何有於不掉之患乎？刑故宥過，而期於無刑，五刑之屬若嚴，五用之法則恕也，何有於禁網之密乎？是即臣所謂大法之立，而為綱紀之振如此，其致雍熙泰和之盛，而為風俗之美也，宜哉！

…with establishments of one hundred, twice that number, or three hundred and sixty officials. Land was allotted to the cultivators, and levies were established to support the governing gentlemen: there were the tribute, labor-assistance, and shared-assessment systems, extending to fifty mu of ritual-support land and twenty-five mu for additional adult males. How comprehensive their arrangements were! Schools were established to make instruction clear, and scholars were nurtured to provide a reserve of talent. There were the schools called xiao, xu, and xiang, extending to the Left School, the Right School, the Yu School, and the State School. Their institutions were complete in every respect. From selection in the village and recommendation by the township to advancement to the royal capital, there were accomplished scholars and scholars presented for appointment; through the Minister of Rites and the Minister of War, they were brought before the king. Once they had been received from all quarters, assigned responsibilities, and appointed at the royal court, their performance was assessed every three years; after three assessments, the unworthy were dismissed and the worthy promoted. Military organization was based on the well-field system, with soldiers incorporated into the farming population. In peacetime they were men who held plows; when trouble arose, they were soldiers who shouldered spears. How could there be any danger of forces becoming too unwieldy to command? Deliberate offenses were punished and inadvertent faults pardoned, with the aim of dispensing with punishments altogether. Although the categories of the Five Punishments seemed severe, the rules for applying them were lenient. How could there be an excessively tight net of prohibitions? This is what your servant means by establishing the great laws and thereby invigorating the governing order. It was fitting that this should produce the flourishing of concord, prosperity, and supreme harmony, and bring refinement to popular customs!

Nevertheless, these were merely the instruments by which they achieved good government. If we trace the foundations of what they established, Yao was able to manifest his lofty virtue; Shun faithfully followed his virtue; Yu reverently put his virtue first; Tang diligently manifested great virtue and established the mean among the people; and Wen and Wu continually cultivated luminous virtue, remained reverent, and established the supreme standard. Which of these lay outside their own persons and minds? If we trace the sequence in which they put this into practice, it extended from the self to the family: giving due order to the nine degrees of kinship, achieving harmony through filial piety, employing those worthy of employment and showing affection to kin, and setting an example for one’s wife. title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
天下為協和萬邦教訖四海克綏厥猷四海永
清也孰有失於徒法徒善者乎篤近以為舉遠
之資由內以為著外之地鼓舞作興之機未嘗
不寓於揆事宰物之中斡旋轉移之妙未嘗不
始於躬行心得之餘然又因時以致其宜隨變
而異其處是以事與時合情隨勢順則其所以
致雍熙泰和之盛而為萬世之法程豈非大幾
之能決有如愚臣所迂論者乎降及後世於漢
則稱七制於唐則稱三宗於宋則稱四聖固皆
創守之賢君也然而致治之效不淪於雜伯則
墮於雜夷不困於西人則擾於北虜小康粗治
雖時時若有可稱而比迹帝王則邈邈乎天壤
異域矣所以然者盖由其狃治功於馬上而詩
書有所不事溺清淨於黃老而制度有所未遑
勵精圖治似矣而多褊察其何以有成躬行仁
義美矣而不克終其何以責効仁厚有餘者不
足於剛武議論繁多者未聞其雄斷任其資以
為治隨其世以就功於
聖制所謂建立之本推行之叙粲乎其有未能若前
所謂綱紀之振而奮發以致治者何有哉宋儒
