天下，為協和萬邦、教訖四海、克綏厥猷、四海永清也。孰有失於徒法徒善者乎？篤近以為舉遠之資，由內以為著外之地，鼓舞作興之機，未嘗不寓於揆事宰物之中；斡旋轉移之妙，未嘗不始於躬行心得之餘。然又因時以致其宜，隨變而異其處，是以事與時合，情隨勢順。則其所以致雍熙泰和之盛，而為萬世之法程，豈非大幾之能決，有如愚臣所迂論者乎？
降及後世，於漢則稱七制，於唐則稱三宗，於宋則稱四聖，固皆創守之賢君也。然而致治之效，不淪於雜伯，則墮於雜夷；不困於西人，則擾於北虜。小康粗治，雖時時若有可稱，而比迹帝王，則邈邈乎天壤異域矣。所以然者，盖由其狃治功於馬上，而詩書有所不事；溺清淨於黃老，而制度有所未遑。勵精圖治似矣，而多褊察，其何以有成？躬行仁義美矣，而不克終，其何以責効？仁厚有餘者，不足於剛武；議論繁多者，未聞其雄斷。任其資以為治，隨其世以就功。於聖制所謂建立之本、推行之叙，粲乎其有未能。若前所謂綱紀之振，而奮發以致治者，何有哉？宋儒
translation_en:
…all under Heaven, this took the form of harmonizing the myriad states, extending instruction throughout the Four Seas, firmly establishing their ways, and bringing lasting peace throughout the Four Seas. Which of these rulers ever fell into the error of relying on laws alone or goodness alone? They devoted themselves to what was near as the means of reaching what was distant, and proceeded from within as the foundation for making virtue manifest without. The means of inspiring and invigorating people were always present in their deliberation over affairs and direction of things; the subtle power to redirect and transform always began with personal practice and inward understanding. Yet they also adapted to the times to achieve what was fitting, and varied their responses as circumstances changed. Thus their actions accorded with the times, and human sentiments followed the course of circumstances harmoniously. Was not their ability to bring about flourishing concord and supreme harmony, and to become models for ten thousand generations, due to their capacity to decide the great pivotal matters, just as your foolish servant has argued in his roundabout way?
Coming down to later ages, people praise the seven reigns of the Han, the three ancestral emperors of the Tang, and the four sage rulers of the Song. These were certainly all worthy sovereigns who founded or preserved their dynasties. Yet the results of their government either sank into an admixture of hegemonic rule or fell into an admixture of barbarian ways; they were either hard-pressed by peoples of the west or harassed by northern invaders. Although their modest prosperity and rudimentary order sometimes seemed praiseworthy, when their achievements are compared with those of the ancient sage emperors and kings, they stand as far apart as heaven and earth, as though belonging to different realms. This was because they were accustomed to achieving rule on horseback and neglected the Odes and the Documents; or they were engrossed in the quietude of the teachings of Huang-Lao and had no leisure to establish institutions and regulations. They seemed to exert themselves in pursuit of good government, but were often narrow-minded and excessively scrutinizing: how could they accomplish anything? Their personal practice of benevolence and righteousness was admirable, but they could not sustain it to the end: how could results be expected? Those amply endowed with benevolence and generosity lacked firmness and martial prowess; those prolific in discussion were never known for bold decisiveness. They relied on their natural endowments to govern and followed the conditions of their age to achieve results. In regard to what Your Majesty’s decree calls the foundation to be established and the sequence of its implementation, they manifestly fell short [?]. As for what was mentioned earlier—revitalizing the governing framework and exerting themselves to bring about good government—what did they have to show? A Confucian scholar of the Song…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
朱熹有曰善為治者必先有綱紀以持之於上
而後有風俗以驅之於下綱紀者何辨賢否以
定上下之分核功罪以公賞罰之施是也風俗
者何使人皆知善之可為而必為皆知不善之
可羞而必去也然綱紀之所以振則以宰執秉
持而不敢失臺諫補察而無所私人主又以大
公至正之心恭已於上而照臨之賞則為予為
陟為三錫而總之為命有功罰則為奪為黜為
五刑而總之為討有罪人君勵世磨鈍以奔走
乎天下之人不越此二事而已曰綱則其大者
===
紀則衆目之小焉綱則貴於常張紀則貴於常
理詩云勉勉我王綱紀四方惟勉勉則所以為
綱紀者至矣世惟賢者弗任而任之或不專否
者弗去而去之或弗决則上下之分不能定有
功者不錄而所錄或非其功有罪者不刑而所
刑或非其罪則賞罰之施有弗公夫用一人焉
賞一人焉而天下以為慶則天下之善有所勸
舍一人焉罰一人焉而天下以為威則天下之
惡有所懲天下之善者勸則天下皆知善之當
為而人人有向善之風薫陶之久漸摩之至雖

…Zhu Xi once said: “Those skilled in governing must first have governing principles and regulations to uphold order above, and then customs to guide the people below. What are governing principles and regulations? They mean distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy to establish the proper distinctions between superior and subordinate, and examining merits and offenses to ensure fairness in administering rewards and punishments. What are customs? They mean causing everyone to know that good should be done and invariably to do it, and to know that wrongdoing is shameful and invariably to abandon it. Governing principles and regulations are kept vigorous when chief councilors uphold them without daring to neglect them, censorial and remonstrance officials remedy omissions and scrutinize faults without partiality, and the ruler, with a supremely impartial and upright mind, maintains a reverent bearing above and watches over all. Rewards take the form of grants, promotions, and threefold bestowals; collectively, these constitute honoring those who have merit. Punishments take the form of deprivation, dismissal, and the five punishments; collectively, these constitute chastising those who are guilty. In spurring on the age and rousing the sluggish, so that all under Heaven exert themselves, the ruler need go no further than these two matters.”
The ‘guiding cord’ (gang) denotes the larger elements of order; the ‘connecting threads’ (ji) are the smaller elements comprising the many meshes of the net. The guiding cord should always be stretched taut, and the connecting threads always kept in order. The Book of Odes says: “Unflagging is our king, ordering and regulating the four quarters.” Only through such unflagging effort can governing principles and regulations be brought to perfection. When the worthy are not appointed, or, if appointed, are not given undivided authority; when the unworthy are not removed, or their removal is pursued indecisively, the proper distinctions between superior and subordinate cannot be established. When those with merit receive no recognition, or recognition is given for something that is not their merit; when the guilty go unpunished, or punishment is imposed for something that is not their offense, rewards and punishments are administered unfairly. If one person is appointed or rewarded and all under Heaven regard it as cause for celebration, goodness throughout the realm receives encouragement. If one person is dismissed or punished and all under Heaven regard it with awe, evil throughout the realm meets a deterrent. When the good throughout the realm are encouraged, everyone knows that good ought to be done, and each person develops an inclination toward goodness. text:
不厚祿高爵以待之自無一人不歸於善天下
之惡者懲則天下皆知惡之不當為而人人有
恥惡之意假以旬時運以德樞雖不嚴刑峻法
以處之自無一人不改其惡夫如是則風俗何
有不醇天下何有不治三代而上正以能此故
爾言漢之綱紀委任大臣掃除煩苛約法減租
綜覈名實律令則命蕭何禮儀則命叔孫通章
程軍法則定於張蒼韓信若曰少振之矣然多
仍秦之舊而衆目猶有未舉言唐之綱紀職事
任官世業任民租庸調任賦府衛彍騎任兵三
===
訊五覆奏任刑禮制於房玄齡樂制於祖孝孫
律令編於長孫無忌若曰亦既張矣然皆襲隋
之餘而大綱猶有未正言宋則刑不加於士夫
事不委於戚畹兵有三衙四廂之制刑有折杖
覆訊之法禮制於劉溫叟樂制於和峴封樁則
有庫審官則有院比之漢唐雖若不同然而六
官無分治之典三考無黜陟之嚴亦惟因五代
之陋習也故其風俗之成止於海內殷富黎民
醇厚而禮義則有未興斗米三錢外戶不閉而
道揆則有未立忠厚廉恥之名文物雖盛而國

不厚祿高爵以待之，自無一人不歸於善。天下之惡者懲，則天下皆知惡之不當為，而人人有恥惡之意。假以旬時，運以德樞，雖不嚴刑峻法以處之，自無一人不改其惡。夫如是，則風俗何有不醇？天下何有不治？三代而上，正以能此故爾。
言漢之綱紀，委任大臣，掃除煩苛，約法減租，綜覈名實。律令則命蕭何，禮儀則命叔孫通，章程軍法則定於張蒼、韓信，若曰少振之矣。然多仍秦之舊，而衆目猶有未舉。言唐之綱紀，職事任官，世業任民，租庸調任賦，府衛彍騎任兵，三訊五覆奏任刑。禮制於房玄齡，樂制於祖孝孫，律令編於長孫無忌，若曰亦既張矣。然皆襲隋之餘，而大綱猶有未正。言宋，則刑不加於士夫，事不委於戚畹。兵有三衙四廂之制，刑有折杖覆訊之法。禮制於劉溫叟，樂制於和峴，封樁則有庫，審官則有院。比之漢唐，雖若不同，然而六官無分治之典，三考無黜陟之嚴，亦惟因五代之陋習也。
故其風俗之成，止於海內殷富、黎民醇厚，而禮義則有未興；斗米三錢、外戶不閉，而道揆則有未立；忠厚廉恥之名，文物雖盛，而國

…even without treating them to generous stipends and high noble rank, naturally not a single person would fail to turn toward goodness. When the wicked throughout the realm are deterred, all under Heaven know that evil ought not to be done, and everyone feels ashamed of wrongdoing. Given some time, and guided by virtue as the pivot of government, even without being subjected to harsh punishments and severe laws, naturally not a single person would fail to reform. If this were so, how could customs fail to be wholesome? How could all under Heaven fail to be well governed? The Three Dynasties and earlier ages achieved this precisely because they could act in this way.
As for the governing framework of the Han, great ministers were entrusted with responsibility, vexatious and oppressive measures were swept away, laws were simplified and taxes reduced, and actual performance was comprehensively checked against nominal responsibilities. Xiao He was charged with statutes and ordinances, and Shusun Tong with ritual and ceremony; regulations and military law were settled by Zhang Cang and Han Xin. One might say that the framework had been somewhat reinvigorated. Yet much of the old Qin system remained, and many of its subsidiary provisions had still not been put into effect. As for the governing framework of the Tang, official service was assigned to officeholders, hereditary landholdings to the people, taxation to the system of grain tax, labor-service commutation, and household levy, military affairs to the militia guards and guoqi cavalry, and penal affairs to triple interrogation and five submissions for imperial review. Ritual was instituted by Fang Xuanling, music by Zu Xiaosun, and statutes and ordinances were compiled by Zhangsun Wuji. One might say that the framework had indeed been established. Yet all this inherited the remnants of the Sui system, and the main principles had still not been rectified. As for the Song, punishments were not inflicted on scholar-officials, and affairs were not entrusted to imperial relatives by marriage. Military organization had the system of the Three Commands and Four Divisions; penal administration had provisions for commuting punishments to beating with the heavy stick and for reviewing interrogations. Ritual was instituted by Liu Wensou, and music by He Xian. There was a treasury for sealed reserves and a Bureau of Personnel Evaluation for assessing officials. Although these arrangements seemed different from those of the Han and Tang, the six ministries lacked rules for a division of administrative responsibilities, and the three successive performance evaluations lacked rigor in demotion and promotion. They merely perpetuated the defective practices of the Five Dynasties.
Thus, the customs they produced amounted only to prosperity within the seas and simplicity and sincerity among the common people, while ritual propriety and righteousness had yet to flourish; rice costing three coins per dou and outer doors left unbarred, while the Way had yet to be established as the measure of government; and a reputation for loyalty, generosity, integrity, and a sense of shame. title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
勢常削弱不振邊事常警報未寧也是豈帝王
之治真不可復盖以賢否倒置賞罰任情致治
之道既虧法制之美奚補無怪乎風俗之美不
如二帝三王也仰惟我
太祖高皇帝肇造區夏創建宏規用夏變夷復綱常
於淪斁之後除殘去暴拯生民於塗炭之餘
太宗文皇帝中靖家邦纂述大統振兵威於四夷而
神武之布昭明理學於萬方而
聖化之覃被其所立之綱紀一皆取法於帝王求端
於天地合德於覆載之公並明於日月之照據
===
今
聖政記及
聖製諸書可以莊誦而考知也故一時之賢者必上
否者必下有功者必賞有罪者必罰以股肱任
宰執而政柄有歸以耳目任臺諫而公議有在
所以治隆俗美醇而不雜比之二帝三王而致
雍熙泰和之盛盖有異世而同歸者矣
列聖相承監於成憲益隆不替歷年百五十餘其道
即所以為治其治即所以為道其教即所以為
政其政即所以為教如古人所謂合一者是也

punctuated:
勢常削弱不振，邊事常警報未寧也。是豈帝王之治真不可復？盖以賢否倒置，賞罰任情，致治之道既虧，法制之美奚補？無怪乎風俗之美不如二帝三王也。
仰惟我太祖高皇帝肇造區夏，創建宏規，用夏變夷，復綱常於淪斁之後，除殘去暴，拯生民於塗炭之餘。太宗文皇帝中靖家邦，纂述大統，振兵威於四夷而神武之布昭，明理學於萬方而聖化之覃被。其所立之綱紀，一皆取法於帝王，求端於天地，合德於覆載之公，並明於日月之照。據今《聖政記》及聖製諸書，可以莊誦而考知也。故一時之賢者必上，否者必下，有功者必賞，有罪者必罰。以股肱任宰執，而政柄有歸；以耳目任臺諫，而公議有在。所以治隆俗美，醇而不雜，比之二帝三王而致雍熙泰和之盛，盖有異世而同歸者矣。
列聖相承，監於成憲，益隆不替。歷年百五十餘，其道即所以為治，其治即所以為道，其教即所以為政，其政即所以為教，如古人所謂合一者是也。
translation_en:
…the power of the state was continually weakened and failed to recover, while repeated alarms left the frontiers unsettled. Could it really be that the government of the ancient emperors and kings could not be restored? Rather, the worthy and unworthy were placed in inverted ranks, and rewards and punishments were dispensed according to personal inclination. Once the Way of achieving good government had been impaired, what could fine laws and institutions remedy? It is no wonder that the excellence of their customs fell short of those under the Two Emperors and Three Kings.
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao founded his rule over the Chinese realm and established a grand design. He transformed the barbarians through Chinese civilization, restored the cardinal bonds and constant virtues after their collapse and corruption, eliminated the cruel and violent, and rescued the people from their suffering. Emperor Taizong Wen pacified the dynastic house and realm within, continued and carried forward the great imperial succession, and made his military might felt among the barbarians of the four quarters, manifesting his divine martial power. He illuminated the Learning of Principle throughout the world, extending his sagely transforming influence far and wide. The governing principles and institutions he established all took the ancient emperors and kings as their models and sought their source in Heaven and Earth. Their virtue accorded with the impartiality of Heaven’s covering and Earth’s sustaining, and their brilliance matched the illumination of the sun and moon. These things can be ascertained through reverent reading and examination of the present Record of Sagely Government (Shengzheng ji) and the various imperially authored works. Thus, the worthy of the time were invariably advanced, the unworthy invariably demoted, those with merit invariably rewarded, and those guilty of wrongdoing invariably punished. The chief councilors were entrusted with service as the ruler’s arms and legs, so that governmental authority had its proper seat; the censorial and remonstrance officials were entrusted with service as his ears and eyes, so that public judgment had a place to be expressed. Consequently, government flourished and customs were excellent, pure and unadulterated. Matching the Two Emperors and Three Kings in achieving abundant concord, prosperity, and profound harmony, they attained the same end in a different age.
The successive sage emperors inherited this legacy, taking established statutes as their guide and further enhancing it without decline. Over more than a hundred and fifty years, their Way has been the means of governing, and their government the means of putting the Way into practice; their teaching has been the means of conducting administration, and their administration the means of teaching. This is what the ancients called their union as one.

text:
故能綱紀有張而不弛風俗一定而不移視之
祖宗之朝則亦無甚相遠
陛下之心即我
祖宗列聖之心即堯舜禹湯文武之心也撫臨億兆

策問臣等使陳其故臣知
陛下此意蓋欲遠追帝王之蹤近光
祖宗之烈不安於漢唐宋之粗治小康明矣臣昔在
巖穴時嘗念有懷而不得申今者接
===

可乎夫綱紀者其先在於辨賢否今之孰賢孰
否

故能綱紀有張而不弛，風俗一定而不移，視之祖宗之朝，則亦無甚相遠。陛下之心，即我祖宗列聖之心，即堯舜禹湯文武之心也。撫臨億兆，夙夜祗懼，圖惟治理，不越以是心布之綱紀而已。然猶惓惓焉，以績效未臻、和氣未應為憂，而策問臣等，使陳其故。臣知陛下此意，蓋欲遠追帝王之蹤，近光祖宗之烈，不安於漢唐宋之粗治小康，明矣。臣昔在巖穴時，嘗念有懷而不得申。今者接咫尺之威，立方寸之地，不為披肝瀝膽以陳於前，可乎？

translation_en:
Thus the guiding principles and ordering rules of government have remained firmly upheld without slackening, and customs have become settled without shifting. Compared with the reigns of the imperial ancestors, there is no great difference. Your Majesty’s heart is the very heart of our imperial ancestors and all the sage emperors, and the very heart of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu. Presiding over the countless multitudes, reverently vigilant day and night and considering how to achieve good government, you do no more than bring this heart to bear upon the guiding principles and ordering rules of government. Yet you remain earnestly concerned that results have not been fully attained and harmonious qi has not responded, and you have put a policy question to us, your servants, asking us to explain the causes. Your servant understands that your intention is to follow the distant footsteps of the ancient emperors and kings and to add lustre to the more recent achievements of your imperial ancestors. Clearly, you are not content with the rudimentary order and modest tranquillity of the Han, Tang, and Song. Formerly, when your servant lived in rustic seclusion, I often reflected that I had thoughts I could not express. Now, standing upon this tiny patch of ground in the immediate presence of your imperial majesty, could I fail to lay bare my innermost thoughts before you?
As for the guiding principles and ordering rules of government, the first requirement is to distinguish the worthy from the unworthy. Who today is worthy and who unworthy—does Your Majesty not know with perfect clarity? Their essential requirement is impartiality in rewards and punishments. In rewarding or punishing today, could Your Majesty entertain any partial judgment? The chief councilors are charged with upholding these principles: would Your Majesty allow them to be unable to carry out their purposes? The censors and remonstrance officials are charged with correcting deficiencies and scrutinizing affairs: would Your Majesty allow them to be unable to speak their minds fully? Why, then, have results not been fully attained and harmonious qi not responded? Where does the fault originate? Your servant ventures to think that the new policies are excellent, but perhaps care has not been sustained through to the end to carry forward the beginning? Veteran ministers have been employed, but perhaps they have not been understood deeply enough or entrusted with sufficiently weighty responsibilities? The people’s afflictions have been removed, but perhaps the responsible officials who exploit and exact from them have not reformed? Affairs…

莠其根猶有尚存者乎四目明矣觀聽左右者

武備所以戡禍亂行伍之法雖具而折衝之精
采未聞或者不免於單弱乎凡此皆大法之所
當急而大幾之決正此時焉夫天下之幾莫大
於維新之日何則君子洗心以改德小人傾耳
===

正事以成嘉靖之休原其理數則否之極而泰
来剥之盡而復生此一幾之先見所當逆決者

之後易以治危之後易以安此一幾之可為所

中興之盛
陛下以嘉靖紀元中興勵志夫今不為當於何時為
punctuated:
弊革矣，小人之窺伺者或未去乎？姦惡誅矣，在柙之虎，其志猶有思騁者乎？巧佞逐矣，亂苗之莠，其根猶有尚存者乎？四目明矣，觀聽左右者或投夫嗜好之機乎？四聰達矣，浮薄競進者或亂夫清穆之道乎？文教所以綏太平，學校之政雖修，而道德之本實未至，或者不免於粉飾乎？武備所以戡禍亂，行伍之法雖具，而折衝之精采未聞，或者不免於單弱乎？凡此皆大法之所當急，而大幾之決，正此時焉。

夫天下之幾，莫大於維新之日。何則？君子洗心以改德，小人傾耳以聽命也。於今之日，蓋又不同。原其時勢，則亂之後易以治，危之後易以安，此一幾之可為，所當速決者也。昔殷高宗承外叛内亂之餘，其時勢正類於此。惟高宗識其幾而決之，故能修德正事，以成嘉靖之休。原其理數，則否之極而泰来，剥之盡而復生，此一幾之先見，所當逆決者也。昔周宣王承人離天變之後，其理數正合於是。惟宣王因其幾而乘之，故能内修外攘，以致中興之盛。

陛下以嘉靖紀元，中興勵志。夫今不為，當於何時為
translation_en:
…abuses have been reformed, yet might petty men who watch for opportunities still remain? The wicked have been executed, yet might these caged tigers still harbor ambitions to run free? The crafty flatterers have been expelled, yet might the roots of these weeds that choke the seedlings still survive? Your sight reaches clearly in all four directions, yet might those who watch and listen at your side exploit openings afforded by your personal tastes? Your hearing reaches in all four directions, yet might frivolous men competing for advancement disrupt the pure and dignified conduct of government? Civil instruction is the means of securing lasting peace. Although the administration of schools has been put in order, the substantial foundation of moral cultivation has not yet been attained: might this still amount to mere embellishment? Military preparedness is the means of suppressing calamity and disorder. Although regulations for the ranks are in place, no vigor capable of repelling aggression has been heard of: might the forces still be weak? All these are urgent concerns of the great principles of government, and this is precisely the moment to act decisively upon the great opportunity.

No opportunity in the realm is greater than the day of renewal. Why? Because gentlemen cleanse their hearts to reform their virtue, while petty men incline their ears to hear commands. Yet the present moment is more exceptional still. Considering the circumstances of the time, order is readily established after disorder, and security after peril. Here is an opportunity for effective action that demands a swift decision. In antiquity, Gaozong of Yin inherited the aftermath of rebellion abroad and disorder within; the circumstances of his time closely resembled those of the present. Because Gaozong recognized his opportunity and acted decisively, he was able to cultivate virtue and set affairs right, achieving the blessing of excellent and tranquil government. Considering the patterns and cycles of events, when Stagnation reaches its extreme, Peace arrives; when Stripping Away is exhausted, Return arises. Here is an opportunity whose first signs can be discerned and which demands a decision in anticipation. In antiquity, King Xuan of Zhou inherited a situation in which the people had become estranged and Heaven had manifested anomalies; its underlying patterns and cycles corresponded exactly to these. Because King Xuan followed and seized his opportunity, he was able to put internal affairs in order and repel external threats, bringing about a flourishing restoration.

Your Majesty has inaugurated the era under the name Jiajing—excellent and tranquil government—and set your resolve upon a restoration. If you do not act now, at what time will you act…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
耶夫事必稽諸古而後有以驗夫因革之宜治
必端其本而後可以不紊夫先後之序誠如
陛下之所諭也古人之行臣既畧陳之矣臣於此又
有端本之說獻焉端本無過於修身講學身者
天下之本而心者又一身之本身之修與不修
在心之正與不正心之正與不正在學之講與
不講講學之道又在乎專於內而無雜於外惟
正心則可以修此身惟講學則可以正此心惟
親君子遠小人則可以專此學學既專則理自
明理既明則事自不眩由是而振綱紀以美風
===
俗賢否自合乎上下之宜功罪自得夫賞罰之
當勸懲所在遠近從風榮辱所激朝夕易俗勵
精有為而期於化行俗美舍此其焉圖之臣願
陛下始終此心而不移緝熈此學而無間持之以悠
久戒之以荒嬉弗溺於宴安罔奪於玩好精擇
善利勇决取舍超然遠覽深惟至計信違拂之
為忠思儆戒之可樂畏天之命悉下之情審時
之宜定
國之是去其不如帝王者以勉夫堯舜禹湯文武
之行檢其不遵成法者以就夫

之行揄其不遵成法者以就夫
punctuated:
耶？夫事必稽諸古，而後有以驗夫因革之宜；治必端其本，而後可以不紊夫先後之序。誠如陛下之所諭也。古人之行，臣既畧陳之矣。臣於此又有端本之說獻焉。端本無過於修身講學。身者天下之本，而心者又一身之本。身之修與不修，在心之正與不正；心之正與不正，在學之講與不講。講學之道，又在乎專於內而無雜於外。惟正心，則可以修此身；惟講學，則可以正此心；惟親君子、遠小人，則可以專此學。學既專，則理自明；理既明，則事自不眩。由是而振綱紀，以美風俗，賢否自合乎上下之宜，功罪自得夫賞罰之當。勸懲所在，遠近從風；榮辱所激，朝夕易俗。勵精有為，而期於化行俗美，舍此其焉圖之？

臣願陛下始終此心而不移，緝熈此學而無間，持之以悠久，戒之以荒嬉，弗溺於宴安，罔奪於玩好，精擇善利，勇决取舍，超然遠覽，深惟至計，信違拂之為忠，思儆戒之可樂，畏天之命，悉下之情，審時之宜，定國之是，去其不如帝王者，以勉夫堯舜禹湯文武之行；檢其不遵成法者，以就夫
translation_en:
…? Affairs must be examined against antiquity before one can assess what should suitably be retained or changed; governance must have its foundation set right before the proper sequence of priorities can be kept from disorder. It is indeed as Your Majesty has instructed. Your servant has already briefly set forth the deeds of the ancients. Here I have a further argument to offer concerning setting the foundation right. Nothing is more essential to this than cultivating oneself and pursuing learning. The self is the foundation of all under Heaven, while the heart is the foundation of the self. Whether the self is cultivated depends on whether the heart is rectified; whether the heart is rectified depends on whether learning is pursued. The way to pursue learning lies in concentrating inwardly, without the intrusion of external distractions. Only by rectifying the heart can one cultivate the self; only by pursuing learning can one rectify the heart; only by drawing close to exemplary men and keeping petty men at a distance can one concentrate on this learning. Once learning is concentrated, principle naturally becomes clear; once principle is clear, one is no longer bewildered by affairs. By proceeding from this to reinvigorate the governing order and improve customs, the worthy and unworthy will naturally receive suitable advancement or demotion, and merit and guilt their appropriate rewards or punishments. Wherever encouragement and chastisement are applied, those near and far will follow their influence; moved by honor and disgrace, people will change their customs overnight. If one strives earnestly to accomplish things, hoping that transforming influence will spread and customs improve, how can this be achieved apart from this course?

Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would remain unwavering in this resolve from beginning to end and continually advance and illuminate this learning without interruption. Sustain it enduringly, guard against idleness and frivolity, do not sink into ease and comfort, and do not let prized amusements divert you. Distinguish carefully between goodness and profit, and decide courageously what to adopt and what to reject. Rise above immediate concerns to take the long view, and ponder deeply the best course. Recognize that opposition to your wishes can be loyalty, and consider admonitions something to welcome. Revere Heaven’s mandate, understand fully the circumstances and sentiments of those below, judge what the times require, and establish what is right for the state. Eliminate whatever falls short of the ancient emperors and kings, striving to emulate the conduct of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu; examine whatever fails to follow established laws, so as to conform to…

translation_en: …the teachings of the imperial ancestors and successive sage sovereigns. You will then see that every undertaking accords with the proper standard and every action brings transformation; achievements will unfailingly follow, and harmonious qi will invariably respond. All the conditions under Heaven that cause concern will thus right themselves without intervention. May Your Majesty graciously accept these proposals and put them into practice. This would be a great blessing for all under Heaven and for ten thousand generations—how could it be a blessing merely for your ignorant servant? Having presumptuously affronted Your Heavenly Majesty, your servant is overwhelmed with trembling fear and dread of falling into ruin. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
臣徐階
臣對臣聞帝王之於天下必稽古以為致治之
資必端本以為出治之地至矣哉古之法乎酌
之於時宜而有以通天下之情致治者之所資
也大矣哉君之心乎斂之於方寸而有以基天
下之化出治者之所本也使人君於此敢於自
用而不知古之當稽則因革之宜必無以驗而
其所設施於是有姦於時者矣惑於他岐而不
知本之當端則先後之序必無以識而其所運
用於是有違於道者矣夫以其姦於時也民將
===
駭之而弗從違於道也民將議之而弗服其何
以一人心厚風俗以成雍熙泰和之盛哉是故
治天下由於法制而惟創於古者不可易也善
為治者必稽諸古昔以為維新之政而不當别

者不可忽也善出治者必求諸此心以為萬化
之本而不當别有所事以為工古焉能稽則因
革之宜可以驗矣本焉能端則先後之序可以
識矣治功之成不由是而可决乎帝王治天下
之道或存乎此而實

punctuated:
臣徐階。

臣對：臣聞帝王之於天下，必稽古以為致治之資，必端本以為出治之地。至矣哉，古之法乎！酌之於時宜，而有以通天下之情，致治者之所資也。大矣哉，君之心乎！斂之於方寸，而有以基天下之化，出治者之所本也。使人君於此敢於自用，而不知古之當稽，則因革之宜必無以驗，而其所設施於是有姦於時者矣；惑於他岐，而不知本之當端，則先後之序必無以識，而其所運用於是有違於道者矣。夫以其姦於時也，民將駭之而弗從；違於道也，民將議之而弗服。其何以一人心、厚風俗，以成雍熙泰和之盛哉？是故治天下由於法制，而惟創於古者不可易也。善為治者，必稽諸古昔，以為維新之政，而不當别有所立以為竒。厚風俗由於紀綱，而惟存諸心者不可忽也。善出治者，必求諸此心，以為萬化之本，而不當别有所事以為工。古焉能稽，則因革之宜可以驗矣；本焉能端，則先後之序可以識矣。治功之成，不由是而可决乎？帝王治天下之道，或存乎此，而實
translation_en:
Your servant Xu Jie.

Your servant replies: I have heard that, in governing all under Heaven, emperors and kings must examine antiquity to obtain the resources for bringing about good government, and must rectify the root to establish the foundation from which government proceeds. How consummate are the methods of antiquity! Adapted to the needs of the times, they enable one to comprehend the circumstances of all under Heaven: these are the resources of those who bring about good government. How great is the ruler’s heart! Concentrated within its tiny compass, it can lay the foundation for the moral transformation of all under Heaven: this is the root upon which those who govern depend.

If a ruler presumes to rely upon his own judgment in these matters, unaware that antiquity must be examined, he will have no means of determining what should appropriately be retained or changed, and the measures he implements will consequently conflict with the needs of the times. If he is misled by divergent paths, unaware that the root must be rectified, he will have no means of discerning the proper order of priorities, and his exercise of government will consequently depart from the Way. Because his measures conflict with the times, the people will be alarmed and refuse to follow them; because they depart from the Way, the people will criticize them and refuse to submit. How, then, can he unite the people’s hearts and improve their customs, bringing about the flourishing condition of concord, prosperity, peace, and harmony?

Thus, governing all under Heaven depends upon laws and institutions, and those established in antiquity must not be altered. Those skilled in governing must examine antiquity to fashion policies of renewal; they should not establish something different merely to display novelty. Improving customs depends upon the guiding principles of order, and what resides in the heart must not be neglected. Those skilled in directing government must seek within this heart the root of all moral transformation; they should not pursue something different merely to display ingenuity. If antiquity can be examined, the appropriate balance between retention and change can be determined. If the root can be rectified, the proper order of priorities can be discerned. Can success in government not thereby be assured? The way in which emperors and kings govern all under Heaven may lie in this, and indeed…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
陛下今日之所欲聞者也恭惟
皇帝陛下剛健中正首出庶物既已具
聖人之德誕膺景命撫有方夏又已得
聖人之時
登極之初渙汗大號與民更始仁澤下流無遠弗
届天下欣欣然有熈皞之樂而公卿大臣百司
庶府亦莫不喜際
昌期勉修職業師師然有讓德之風臣愚以為唐
虞三代
祖宗之時莫是過矣
===
虚懷謙冲不自滿假恒以績效未臻和氣未應為
懼爰進臣等于
廷詢之治道是即望道未見之心取人為善之量
也昔宋儒程顥嘗上稽古之論而朱熹亦每為
正心之言臣愚誦法程朱久矣敢不掇拾一二
以仰副
清問之勤乎竊惟天下至大也兆民至眾也而天
下之俗又不能以皆醇也人君以一人之身尊
臨乎其上非有法制以齊之則民將無所于守
而其渙者不可一非有紀綱以持之則民將莫

translation_en:
…what Your Majesty wishes to hear today. I respectfully consider that Your Imperial Majesty, firm and vigorous, balanced and upright, stands foremost among all beings and already possesses the virtue of a sage. Having grandly received Heaven’s glorious mandate and assumed rule over the Chinese realm, you have also obtained a sage’s opportunity to act. At the beginning of your accession, you issued a great proclamation, irrevocable as sweat once shed, to make a fresh beginning together with the people. Your benevolent blessings flowed down, reaching even the remotest places, and all under Heaven rejoiced in the happiness of radiant harmony. The dukes, ministers, high officials, and all the offices likewise rejoiced to encounter this flourishing age. They diligently attended to their duties, showing mutual deference and a spirit of virtuous yielding. Your foolish servant believes that even the ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, the Three Dynasties, and your imperial ancestors did not surpass this.

Yet you remain open-minded and humble, without complacency, constantly apprehensive that achievements have not yet reached fulfillment and that harmonious influences have not yet responded. You have therefore brought us, your servants, into court and questioned us about the Way of governing. This is precisely the disposition of one who seeks the Way as though he has not yet seen it, and the magnanimity of one who draws upon others to practice goodness. Formerly, the Song scholar Cheng Hao presented a discourse on examining antiquity, while Zhu Xi also repeatedly spoke of rectifying the mind. Your foolish servant has long studied and taken Cheng and Zhu as his models. How could I dare fail to gather one or two of their teachings to meet your earnest and discerning inquiry?

I humbly reflect that the realm is exceedingly vast and its people exceedingly numerous, while its customs cannot all be wholesome. The ruler, in his single person, presides augustly over them. Unless there are laws and institutions to bring them into order, the people will have nothing to observe, and those who are scattered cannot be united. Unless there are governing principles and proper order to hold them together, the people will not…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
知所向而其薄者不可醇古帝王知其然是故
順時揆事創制立法以盡天下之務而莫或叅
之以已意之私綱焉常張紀焉常理以善天下
之俗而尤致謹於本原之地盖其法制之行必
期於可久故其於時宜也自不容有所違紀綱
之立必期於成化故其於心術也自不容有所
忽其所以率天下於王道之中囿民生於帝則
之内者夫豈苟然之故哉臣請自其法制言之
禮之定也有吉凶軍賓嘉之興而神人治焉樂
之定也有章韶夏濩武之異而上下和焉黃鍾
===
太簇姑洗蕤賓夷則無射以為陽太吕夾鍾仲
吕林鍾南吕應鍾以為陰則律明而度量衡於
此乎興璿璣玉衡以齊七政步推積分以立閏
法則曆明而民時於是乎授疆理宇内則或肇
之為十二州或合之為九州或第之為五服而
疆界昭設立庶官則或稽古建官惟百或官倍
亦克用乂或三百六十統於六卿而政教舉咸
則三壤任土作貢百里賦納總二百里納銍三
百里納秸服四百里粟五百里米以至貢助徹
各一其法而所以分田制賦者為甚周春秋教

呂林鍾南呂應鍾以為陰則律明而度量衡於
此乎興璿璣玉衡以齊七政步推積分以立閏

之為十二州或合之為九州或第之為五服而
疆界昭設立庶官則或稽古建官惟百或官倍
亦克用乂或三百六十統於六卿而政教舉咸
則三壤任土作貢百里賦納總二百里納銍三
百里納秸服四百里粟五百里米以至貢助徹
各一其法而所以分田制賦者為甚周春秋教
punctuated:
知所向，而其薄者不可醇。古帝王知其然，是故順時揆事，創制立法，以盡天下之務，而莫或叅之以已意之私。綱焉常張，紀焉常理，以善天下之俗，而尤致謹於本原之地。盖其法制之行，必期於可久，故其於時宜也，自不容有所違；紀綱之立，必期於成化，故其於心術也，自不容有所忽。其所以率天下於王道之中，囿民生於帝則之内者，夫豈苟然之故哉！臣請自其法制言之。
禮之定也，有吉凶軍賓嘉之興，而神人治焉；樂之定也，有章韶夏濩武之異，而上下和焉。黃鍾、太簇、姑洗、蕤賓、夷則、無射以為陽，太吕、夾鍾、仲吕、林鍾、南吕、應鍾以為陰，則律明，而度量衡於此乎興。璿璣玉衡，以齊七政；步推積分，以立閏法，則曆明，而民時於是乎授。疆理宇内，則或肇之為十二州，或合之為九州，或第之為五服，而疆界昭。設立庶官，則或稽古建官惟百，或官倍亦克用乂，或三百六十統於六卿，而政教舉。咸則三壤，任土作貢，百里賦納總，二百里納銍，三百里納秸服，四百里粟，五百里米，以至貢、助、徹，各一其法，而所以分田制賦者為甚周。春秋教
translation_en:
…know where to turn, and those whose customs are shallow cannot be made upright. The ancient emperors and kings understood this. Accordingly, they followed the times and assessed affairs, creating institutions and establishing laws to encompass all the business of the realm, without introducing the selfish preferences of their own will. They kept the guiding cords constantly taut and the lesser threads constantly ordered, thereby improving the customs of the realm, and exercised particular care over their foundations. In implementing institutions and laws, they aimed invariably at enduring effectiveness; thus they could permit no departure from what the times required. In establishing the guiding principles of government, they aimed invariably at achieving moral transformation; thus they could permit no neglect of the workings of the heart. Could their means of leading the realm along the Kingly Way and keeping the people’s lives within the standards of the ancient emperors have been merely haphazard? Allow your servant to begin with their institutions and laws.
When rites were established, the rites for auspicious occasions, mourning, military affairs, receiving guests, and celebrations were instituted, bringing order to relations between spirits and humans. When music was established, the distinct forms of Zhang [?], Shao, Xia, Huo, and Wu brought harmony between those above and below. Huangzhong, Taicu, Guxian, Ruibin, Yize, and Wuyi were designated yang; Dalü, Jiazhong, Zhonglü, Linzhong, Nanlü, and Yingzhong were designated yin. The pitch standards were thereby clarified, and standards of length, capacity, and weight arose from them. The jade celestial instrument and jade sighting tube were used to bring the seven celestial regulators—the sun, moon, and five planets—into accord. Calculating their motions and accumulating fractional remainders established the method of intercalation. The calendar was thereby clarified, and the proper seasons for the people’s work were announced.
In demarcating the realm, they sometimes first established twelve provinces, sometimes combined them into nine provinces, and sometimes ranked the territories into five zones of service, making the boundaries clear. In establishing the various offices, they sometimes followed antiquity and appointed only a hundred officials; sometimes doubled that number and still achieved orderly government; and sometimes placed three hundred and sixty offices under the Six Ministers. Government and moral instruction were thus put into effect.
They everywhere followed the classification of soils into three grades and assessed tribute according to the land. Within the first hundred li, the levy was delivered as whole grain plants; within the second hundred li, as cut ears; within the third hundred li, as grain with the stalks removed; within the fourth hundred li, as unhusked grain; and within the fifth hundred li, as husked grain. Likewise, the gong, zhu, and che systems of taxation each had their own established method. Their arrangements for allocating fields and regulating levies were thus exceedingly thorough. In spring and autumn, instruction…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
以禮樂冬夏教以詩書曰小學在公宮南之左大
學在郊天子曰辟雝諸侯曰頖宮以至庠序校
各一其名而所以興學養士者為甚備敷奏以
言明試以功三載考績三考黜陟幽明鄉舉里
選之惟公秀造俊進之有等是皆所謂選舉考
課之法也司馬掌邦政統六師平邦國司寇掌
邦禁詰姦慝刑暴亂是皆所謂兵戎刑罰之制
也建立有本而近不出於人君之身推行有序
而漸以達於天下之大則固足以成治於一時
而凡後世之則亦有不能外焉者矣夫何自秦
===
以降事不師古雖其間號稱善治如漢唐宋者
英君誼辟往往作於創業守成之時而究其建
立終不能彷彿於帝王之盛如漢之七制非不
有可稱也然禮文雜就於秦儀之陋律令捃摭
乎秦法之遺章程定而闊疏之弊猶存軍法申
而九伐之義亦昧賢良舉矣不知有學校之當
先民租減矣不知有井田之當復芝房寶鼎之
歌何取乎音樂之正珠崖大宛之戰何取乎弔
伐之師戶口偽增以蒙上賞既非考課之嚴不
任三公事歸臺閣尤非設官之意則夫兩漢之

punctuated:
以禮樂，冬夏教以詩書。曰小學在公宮南之左，大學在郊；天子曰辟雝，諸侯曰頖宮，以至庠序校，各一其名，而所以興學養士者為甚備。敷奏以言，明試以功，三載考績，三考黜陟幽明；鄉舉里選之惟公，秀造俊進之有等，是皆所謂選舉考課之法也。司馬掌邦政，統六師，平邦國；司寇掌邦禁，詰姦慝，刑暴亂，是皆所謂兵戎刑罰之制也。建立有本，而近不出於人君之身；推行有序，而漸以達於天下之大，則固足以成治於一時，而凡後世之則，亦有不能外焉者矣。
夫何自秦以降，事不師古？雖其間號稱善治如漢唐宋者，英君誼辟往往作於創業守成之時，而究其建立，終不能彷彿於帝王之盛。如漢之七制，非不有可稱也，然禮文雜就於秦儀之陋，律令捃摭乎秦法之遺。章程定而闊疏之弊猶存，軍法申而九伐之義亦昧。賢良舉矣，不知有學校之當先；民租減矣，不知有井田之當復。芝房寶鼎之歌，何取乎音樂之正？珠崖大宛之戰，何取乎弔伐之師？戶口偽增以蒙上賞，既非考課之嚴；不任三公，事歸臺閣，尤非設官之意。則夫兩漢之
translation_en:
…with rites and music, while in winter and summer they were taught the Odes and Documents. It is said that the elementary school stood to the left of the southern side of the ducal palace, and the great school in the suburbs. The Son of Heaven’s school was called the Biyong, and those of the regional lords were called Pangong; down to the xiang, xu, and xiao schools, each had its own designation. Thus the arrangements for promoting learning and nurturing scholars were most complete. Officials presented their accounts in words and were clearly tested through their accomplishments. Their performance was evaluated every three years, and after three evaluations the unworthy were demoted and the worthy promoted. Recommendations from townships and selections from villages were strictly impartial, while the advancement of outstanding and accomplished scholars proceeded through graded stages. These were all what are called methods of selection and performance evaluation. The Minister of War directed the state’s military administration, commanded the six armies, and pacified the states. The Minister of Justice administered the state’s prohibitions, investigated wickedness, and punished violence and disorder. These were all what are called institutions of warfare and punishment. Their establishment had a foundation close at hand, extending no further than the ruler’s own person; their implementation followed an orderly sequence, gradually reaching throughout the vast realm. They were certainly sufficient to achieve good government in their own time, and among the standards of later generations there were likewise those that could not depart from them.
Why, then, from the Qin onward, did affairs cease to take antiquity as their model? Even under such dynasties as the Han, Tang, and Song, reputed for good government, enlightened rulers and righteous sovereigns frequently arose both at their founding and during the preservation of their achievements. Yet when one examines the institutions they established, these ultimately could not approach the flourishing order of the ancient emperors and kings. The seven exemplary Han reigns were certainly not without praiseworthy features. Yet their ceremonial forms were pieced together from the crude observances of the Qin, and their statutes and ordinances were gleaned from remnants of Qin law. Regulations were established, but the defects of laxity and incompleteness remained; military law was reiterated, but the principles governing the nine grounds for punitive expeditions remained obscure. Men of worth and ability were recommended, yet it was not understood that schools should come first. The people’s land taxes were reduced, yet it was not understood that the well-field system ought to be restored. What did the songs “The Chamber of Auspicious Fungi” and “The Precious Tripod” have to do with correct music? What did the campaigns against Zhuya and Dayuan have to do with armies sent to succor the afflicted and punish the guilty? Household and population figures were fraudulently inflated to obtain rewards from above: this hardly constituted rigorous performance evaluation. Responsibility was withheld from the Three Dukes, and affairs were entrusted to the Secretariat: this departed still further from the purpose of establishing offices. Thus, the rule of the two Han dynasties …

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
治所以病於雜霸狃於小康剛者蹈急迫之虞
柔者貽寬縱之失有由然也唐之三宗非不有
可稱也然貞觀開元之禮具其文而意不在特
所謂虛名者耳棃園小部之樂啻足為戒而不
足考法盖所謂新聲者耳曆之作凡二十三家
而不免愈密愈差之議官之建凡七百三十而
不免員外置特置之繁大徵天下名儒為學官
似矣顧學士能通一經以上即得補官屯營飛
騎有能通經者即得貢舉而無復聖賢明德新
民之學生徒鄉貢制舉以取士幾矣顧為進士
===
===
者皆誦當代之文而不通經史明經者但記帖
括又投牒自舉而非復哲王仄席待賢之道口
分世業以養民而什一之規猶未備設府立衞
以聚兵而藩鎮之防猶未密善最之法廢而其
後也至於限年躡級無得踰越才俊之士無不
怨歎律令之格式廢而其末也至於刑書繁雜
精明之士不能遍習吏得上下以為姦則夫唐
之為治所以病於假仁流於雜夷有盈成之業
而不能守有恢復之功而不克終固其宜也宋
之太祖太宗仁宗又非不有可稱也然以開寶

怨歎律令之格式廢而其末也至於刑書繁雜
精明之士不能遍習吏得上下以為姦則夫唐
之為治所以病於假仁流於雜夷有盜成之業
而不能守有恢復之功而不克終固其宜也宋
之太祖太宗仁宗又非不有可稱也然以開寶
punctuated:
治所以病於雜霸、狃於小康，剛者蹈急迫之虞，柔者貽寬縱之失，有由然也。

唐之三宗，非不有可稱也。然貞觀、開元之禮，具其文而意不在，特所謂虛名者耳。棃園小部之樂，啻足為戒而不足考法，盖所謂新聲者耳。曆之作凡二十三家，而不免愈密愈差之議；官之建凡七百三十，而不免員外置、特置之繁。大徵天下名儒為學官，似矣，顧學士能通一經以上即得補官，屯營飛騎有能通經者即得貢舉，而無復聖賢明德新民之學。生徒、鄉貢、制舉以取士，幾矣，顧為進士者皆誦當代之文而不通經史，明經者但記帖括，又投牒自舉，而非復哲王仄席待賢之道。口分、世業以養民，而什一之規猶未備；設府立衞以聚兵，而藩鎮之防猶未密。善最之法廢，而其後也至於限年躡級，無得踰越，才俊之士無不怨歎；律令之格式廢，而其末也至於刑書繁雜，精明之士不能遍習，吏得上下以為姦。則夫唐之為治，所以病於假仁、流於雜夷，有盈成之業而不能守，有恢復之功而不克終，固其宜也。

宋之太祖、太宗、仁宗，又非不有可稱也。然以開寶
translation_en:
…There were thus reasons why the government of the two Han dynasties suffered from an admixture of hegemonic practices and became complacent with modest prosperity: forceful rulers risked excessive haste and pressure, while mild rulers left behind the faults of laxity and indulgence.

The three Tang emperors were not without praiseworthy achievements. Yet the rites of the Zhenguan and Kaiyuan eras possessed the outward forms without their underlying intent; they were merely what is called an empty name. The music of the Pear Garden’s small ensemble served only as a warning, not as a model to study and follow: it was what is called novel music. Twenty-three schools produced calendars, yet they could not escape the criticism that greater precision brought greater error. Seven hundred and thirty official posts were established, yet they could not escape the proliferation of supernumerary and specially created appointments. Summoning renowned Confucian scholars from throughout the realm to serve as education officials seemed right. Yet students who could master one or more classics could immediately receive official appointments, and men in the garrison camps and Flying Cavalry who could master a classic could immediately be recommended for examination. There was no longer the learning of the sages and worthies, which illuminates luminous virtue and renews the people. Recruiting men through government-school students, local tribute candidates, and special examinations came close to the ideal. Yet candidates for the jinshi degree all recited contemporary writings without understanding the classics and histories; candidates in the Mingjing, or Classics Elucidation, examination merely memorized passages for the text-completion tests. Moreover, they submitted documents to nominate themselves: this was no longer the way of wise kings, who sat at the edge of their seats awaiting worthy men.

Land allotted per person and land held hereditarily provided for the people, yet the rule of taxing one part in ten was still not fully established. Military headquarters and guards were established to assemble troops, yet safeguards against the regional military commands remained inadequate. The system of assessing officials by their virtues and achievements fell into disuse. Eventually, promotion proceeded by prescribed years of service and successive grades, with no one permitted to skip a rank; talented men all complained and lamented. The statutes governing the application of laws and ordinances fell into disuse. In the end, penal writings became so numerous and confused that even men of keen understanding could not study them all, and clerks could manipulate their application to commit abuses. Thus Tang government suffered from a pretense of benevolence and drifted into an admixture of barbarian practices. That it possessed a flourishing, established realm but could not preserve it, and achieved restoration but could not carry it through, was surely to be expected.

The Song emperors Taizu, Taizong, and Renzong were likewise not without praiseworthy achievements. Yet, taking the Kaibao …

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
之通禮而擬諸五禮則其得失何如以和峴之
雅樂而比諸六樂則其優劣何如胡瑗房庶之
律均無以得聲氣之元崇天奉元之曆舉無以
窺羲和之妙輕節度之任雖足以戢姦雄之變
而漸無以禦外敵之驕賑諸州之粟雖足以蘇
饑饉之憂而終不能易兩稅之弊覆試嚴而詩
賦之習未改於前時學校建而蘇湖之教未洽
於天下其於考課則司馬光以為采名不采實
誅文不誅意而吏多偷惰之風其於兵戎則范
鎮以為中書主民樞密主兵而事多杆格之患
===
知官之當審而材任相違職政廢弛知刑之當
恤而冤結不理姦暴不除則宋之為治所以因
循苟且日入於弊內無以清朝廷之姦外無以
杜邊埸之釁又何怪其然哉
聖策以為致治之道不專恃於法制是則固然而臣
愚竊敢謂漢唐宋殆併其法制而亡之者耳至
於紀綱風俗則朱熹之論嘗曰善為治者必先
有紀綱以持之於上而後有風俗以驅之於下
何謂紀綱覈功罪以公賞罰之施辨賢否以定
上下之分是也何謂風俗使人曉然知善之可

卹而冤結不理姦暴不除則宋之為治所以因
循苟且日入於弊內無以清朝廷之姦外無以
杜邉場之釁又何怪其然哉

於紀綱風俗則朱熹之論嘗曰善為治者必先
有紀綱以持之於上而後有風俗以驅之於下
何謂紀綱辨賢否以定上下之分覈功罪以公賞罰之施
上下之分是也何謂風俗使人曉然知善之可
punctuated:
之通禮而擬諸五禮，則其得失何如？以和峴之雅樂而比諸六樂，則其優劣何如？胡瑗、房庶之律均，無以得聲氣之元；崇天、奉元之曆，舉無以窺羲和之妙。輕節度之任，雖足以戢姦雄之變，而漸無以禦外敵之驕；賑諸州之粟，雖足以蘇饑饉之憂，而終不能易兩稅之弊。覆試嚴，而詩賦之習未改於前時；學校建，而蘇湖之教未洽於天下。其於考課，則司馬光以為采名不采實，誅文不誅意，而吏多偷惰之風；其於兵戎，則范鎮以為中書主民，樞密主兵，而事多杆格之患。知官之當審，而材任相違，職政廢弛；知刑之當恤，而冤結不理，姦暴不除。則宋之為治，所以因循苟且，日入於弊，內無以清朝廷之姦，外無以杜邊埸之釁，又何怪其然哉？
聖策以為致治之道不專恃於法制，是則固然。而臣愚竊敢謂漢、唐、宋殆併其法制而亡之者耳。至於紀綱風俗，則朱熹之論嘗曰：「善為治者，必先有紀綱以持之於上，而後有風俗以驅之於下。」何謂紀綱？覈功罪以公賞罰之施，辨賢否以定上下之分，是也。何謂風俗？使人曉然知善之可
translation_en:
…Comprehensive Rites of the Kaibao era: when measured against the Five Rites, what were its merits and shortcomings? When He Xian’s ceremonial music is compared with the Six Music Traditions, how does it fare? The pitch standards and tuning systems of Hu Yuan and Fang Shu could not grasp the ultimate source of sound and vital breath; the Chongtian and Fengyuan calendars alike could not fathom the subtleties of Xi and He’s calendrical arts. Reducing the authority of military commissioners sufficed to restrain rebellions by ambitious strongmen, yet gradually left the state unable to resist the insolence of foreign enemies. Distributing grain in relief throughout the prefectures sufficed to alleviate the distress of famine, yet ultimately failed to remedy the abuses of the twice-yearly tax. Reexaminations were strict, but the earlier emphasis on poetry and rhapsodies remained unchanged. Schools were established, but the teaching methods of Suzhou and Huzhou did not spread throughout the realm. Regarding performance evaluations, Sima Guang held that they attended to reputation rather than actual achievement, censuring the written wording rather than the underlying intent; officials were consequently much given to shirking and indolence. Regarding military affairs, Fan Zhen held that the Secretariat administered the people while the Bureau of Military Affairs administered the troops, so that affairs frequently suffered from mutual obstruction. They knew that official appointments required careful scrutiny, yet abilities and assignments were mismatched, and official duties and administration fell into neglect. They knew that punishments required compassionate care, yet unresolved injustices went unredressed, and the wicked and violent were not eliminated. Thus Song government followed established routines and relied on expedients, sinking daily into greater dysfunction. At home it could not purge the court of wickedness; abroad it could not prevent conflict on the frontiers. What wonder that things turned out as they did?
Your Majesty’s policy question holds that the way to achieve good government does not depend exclusively on laws and institutions. This is certainly so. Yet I, your ignorant servant, venture privately to suggest that the Han, Tang, and Song all but lost even their laws and institutions. As for governing discipline and social customs, Zhu Xi once argued: “Those skilled in governing must first have governing discipline to uphold order above, and then social customs to guide people below.” What is meant by governing discipline? It means examining achievements and offenses to ensure impartial rewards and punishments, and distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy to determine their respective places above and below. What is meant by social customs? It means enabling people clearly to understand that goodness is worthy of…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
慕而必爲不善之可羞而必去是也夫以天下
之治本於紀綱而成於風俗則朝廷之上所以
轉移振舉誠莫有急於此者顧惟風俗不能以
徒善而必由於紀綱紀綱不能以自立而必由
於人主之心術唐虞三代其所以爲心術焉者
曰允執厥中曰惟精惟一曰祗台德先曰制事
制心曰緝熈敬止曰建其有極方寸隱微之間
粹然無偏黨反側之累而心術之正何如也故
其體之於身則爲德行措之於政則爲紀綱示
民以所當務而自不昧於所從示民以所不爲
===
而自不迷於所適以黎民則於變以四方則風
動以聲教則四訖以萬邦則惟懷以萬民則咸
和以四海則永清人人君子比屋可封而風俗
之醇何如也自漢以來則紀綱之張弛代有不
同而風俗之醇雜亦遂因之以異此豈紀綱之
不可振風俗之不可醇哉亦由諸君之心術或
不事詩書或喜談佛老而未聞所以養之之方
或仁義外施或德教不醇而未嘗致其養之之
實才明勇畧者不能無溺於圖讖功德兼隆者
不能無愧於躬行勵精政事而卒無以勝其侈

punctuated: 慕而必爲，不善之可羞而必去，是也。夫以天下之治本於紀綱而成於風俗，則朝廷之上所以轉移振舉，誠莫有急於此者。顧惟風俗不能以徒善，而必由於紀綱；紀綱不能以自立，而必由於人主之心術。唐虞三代，其所以爲心術焉者，曰「允執厥中」，曰「惟精惟一」，曰「祗台德先」，曰「制事制心」，曰「緝熈敬止」，曰「建其有極」。方寸隱微之間，粹然無偏黨反側之累，而心術之正何如也！故其體之於身則爲德行，措之於政則爲紀綱。示民以所當務，而自不昧於所從；示民以所不爲，而自不迷於所適。以黎民則於變，以四方則風動，以聲教則四訖，以萬邦則惟懷，以萬民則咸和，以四海則永清。人人君子，比屋可封，而風俗之醇何如也！自漢以來，則紀綱之張弛代有不同，而風俗之醇雜亦遂因之以異。此豈紀綱之不可振、風俗之不可醇哉？亦由諸君之心術，或不事詩書，或喜談佛老，而未聞所以養之之方；或仁義外施，或德教不醇，而未嘗致其養之之實。才明勇畧者，不能無溺於圖讖；功德兼隆者，不能無愧於躬行；勵精政事，而卒無以勝其侈
translation_en:
…worthy of admiration and therefore necessarily to be practiced, and that wrongdoing is shameful and therefore necessarily to be abandoned: this is what is meant. Since the ordering of the realm is rooted in governing discipline and brought to fulfillment through social customs, nothing is more urgent at court than to transform and revitalize these. Yet social customs cannot be made good merely through good intentions; they must depend upon governing discipline. Governing discipline cannot establish itself; it must depend upon the disposition of the ruler’s mind. Under Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, the principles governing that disposition were expressed thus: “Truly hold fast to the Mean”; “Be discerning and single-minded”; “Reverently put my virtue first”; “Regulate affairs and regulate the mind”; “Continue in illumination and abide in reverence”; and “Establish the highest standard.” In the hidden recesses of their hearts, they were utterly pure, unburdened by partiality, factionalism, or inconstancy. How upright was the disposition of their minds! Thus, embodied in their persons, it became virtuous conduct; applied to government, it became governing discipline. They showed the people what they should pursue, and the people naturally understood what to follow; they showed the people what they should refrain from doing, and the people naturally knew which way to turn. The common people were transformed; the four quarters responded as though stirred by the wind; their renown and teaching reached every quarter; the myriad states cherished them; all the people lived in harmony; and all within the Four Seas enjoyed lasting peace. Everyone was a gentleman, and every household had someone worthy of enfeoffment. How pure were their customs!

Since the Han, governing discipline has varied from dynasty to dynasty in its rigor and laxity, and social customs have accordingly differed in their purity or admixture. Could this mean that governing discipline cannot be revitalized or that customs cannot be purified? It results instead from the dispositions of the various rulers’ minds. Some did not devote themselves to the Odes and the Documents; some delighted in discussing Buddhism and Laozi’s teachings, without ever learning the proper means of cultivating their minds. Some displayed benevolence and righteousness only outwardly; some were impure in their moral instruction, without ever realizing the substance of such cultivation. Those endowed with talent, intelligence, courage, and strategic ability could not avoid becoming immersed in prophetic charts and prognostications; those eminent alike in achievement and virtue could not avoid grounds for shame in their personal conduct. Others applied themselves earnestly to affairs of government, yet ultimately could not overcome their extravagance…

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
泰之私防非窒慾而卒莫能進於誠正之域仁
恕恭儉有帝王之畧矣而其所務僅止於讀書
之勤寬仁慈愛有帝王之量矣而其所為不免
於道教之蔽此其心術胡可齒於唐虞三代而
欲紀綱風俗之無弊哉是故漢以規模為紀綱
唐以法度為紀綱宋以忠厚廉恥為紀綱雖若
宋愈於漢漢愈於唐至其視五子之所歌棫樸
之所咏則同邈乎其不逮矣西漢尚經術而習
俗胥靡以至貢符獻瑞失之於詭隨東漢尚節
義而互相標榜以至捐身僨事失之於矯激唐
===
則藩鎮阻兵而君臣之倫缺士卒逐帥而上下
之義乖宋則慶曆以前抑奔競黜浮薄而其俗
每依於厚慶曆以降勸名節敢言事而其俗多
主於剛雖若宋類於漢漢愈於唐而其視康衢
之所謠典謨之所載則均之莫能及矣夫其上
下相承之機彼此感應之理其微不可測而其
徵不可誣如此是豈可不慎哉善乎熹之言曰
紀綱所以振舉在於宰執秉持而無所失臺諫
補察而無所私人主以大公至正之心恭已照
臨於上則夫欲振天下之紀綱以成天下之風

泰之私，防非窒慾，而卒莫能進於誠正之域。仁恕恭儉，有帝王之畧矣，而其所務僅止於讀書之勤；寬仁慈愛，有帝王之量矣，而其所為不免於道教之蔽。此其心術胡可齒於唐虞三代，而欲紀綱風俗之無弊哉？是故漢以規模為紀綱，唐以法度為紀綱，宋以忠厚廉恥為紀綱。雖若宋愈於漢，漢愈於唐，至其視五子之所歌、棫樸之所咏，則同邈乎其不逮矣。西漢尚經術，而習俗胥靡，以至貢符獻瑞，失之於詭隨；東漢尚節義，而互相標榜，以至捐身僨事，失之於矯激；唐則藩鎮阻兵，而君臣之倫缺，士卒逐帥，而上下之義乖；宋則慶曆以前，抑奔競，黜浮薄，而其俗每依於厚，慶曆以降，勸名節，敢言事，而其俗多主於剛。雖若宋類於漢，漢愈於唐，而其視康衢之所謠、典謨之所載，則均之莫能及矣。夫其上下相承之機、彼此感應之理，其微不可測，而其徵不可誣如此，是豈可不慎哉？
善乎熹之言曰：「紀綱所以振舉，在於宰執秉持而無所失，臺諫補察而無所私，人主以大公至正之心，恭已照臨於上。」則夫欲振天下之紀綱，以成天下之風

…the selfish indulgence of extravagance. They guarded against wrongdoing and restrained desire, yet ultimately could not advance into the realm of sincerity and rectitude. Some possessed benevolence, forbearance, reverence, and frugality—the qualities of imperial rule—yet their efforts extended only to diligent reading. Others possessed generosity, humanity, kindness, and affection—the magnanimity of an emperor—yet their conduct remained clouded by Daoist teachings. How could their dispositions of mind rank alongside those of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, and how could they expect the guiding principles of government and prevailing customs to be free of defects?
Thus the Han took its institutional framework as its guiding principles, the Tang its laws and regulations, and the Song loyalty, generosity, integrity, and a sense of shame. Although the Song might appear superior to the Han, and the Han superior to the Tang, measured against what the Five Sons sang and what is celebrated in The Luxuriant Oaks (Yupu), all alike fell far short. The Western Han esteemed classical learning, but prevailing customs deteriorated together [?], even to the presentation of auspicious tokens and portents: its failing was servile compliance. The Eastern Han esteemed moral integrity and righteousness, but men promoted one another’s reputations, even to the point of sacrificing their lives and ruining affairs: its failing was affected extremism. Under the Tang, regional military commands relied on armed force, impairing the proper relationship between ruler and minister; soldiers drove out their commanders, violating the duties binding superiors and subordinates. Under the Song, before the Qingli era, competitive pursuit of advancement was checked and frivolous men dismissed, so prevailing customs generally tended toward sincerity and generosity. From Qingli onward, reputation and integrity were encouraged, together with boldness in discussing public affairs, so prevailing customs chiefly favored firmness. Although the Song might appear comparable to the Han, and the Han superior to the Tang, measured against what was sung on the broad thoroughfare and what is recorded in the Canons and Counsels, none could match them.
Such are the workings by which those above and below sustain one another, and the principles by which each influences and responds to the other: their subtleties cannot be fathomed, yet their manifestations cannot be denied. How could one fail to exercise care?
Well did Zhu Xi say: “The revitalization of the guiding principles of government depends upon chief councilors maintaining them without failure, censorial and remonstrance officials correcting omissions and scrutinizing conduct without partiality, and the ruler, with a mind of supreme impartiality and perfect rectitude, reverently ordering himself and watching over all from above.” Thus, those who wish to revitalize the guiding principles of government throughout the realm and thereby perfect the realm’s customs…

…customs: although the chief councilors and the censorial and remonstrance officials should each discharge their respective duties, the foundation truly lies in the ruler’s own mind. Without utter impartiality, there is no way to eliminate selfishness throughout the realm; without perfect rectitude, there is no way to halt its wickedness. If the ruler is selfish and wicked, his punishments, rewards, and actions cannot help departing from the Way, and customs follow accordingly. Were not the differences between the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, and those of Han, Tang, and Song, precisely due to this?
Reverently considering our Emperor Taizu Gao, he founded his rule over the Chinese realm and established far-reaching institutions. He ordered Niu Liang to formulate the rites, thereby sweeping away corrupt practices, and ordered Tao Kai to establish music, thereby entirely banishing licentious and indecent sounds. The calendar followed the established system of the preceding dynasty, while the pitch standards adopted earlier Song precedents. Through thirteen Provincial Administration Commissions, he divided responsibility for governing the realm, accommodating the configurations and advantages of its mountains and rivers [?]; through the Duties of the Various Offices, he coordinated all officials, so that those at the capital and in the provinces, of greater and lesser rank, sustained one another. Land taxes had fixed quotas, and powerful magnates could not engross land; performance evaluations had established rules, and the worthy and unworthy could not be confused. As soon as warfare had subsided, schools were established; regular channels for examination and tribute recruitment ensured that worthy and capable men were periodically recommended.
He ordered Minister Liu Weiqian to bring together the various statutes and harmonize them with the proper mean, correcting the faults of recent reliance on analogies and precedents. He instructed the officials of the Branch Secretariat to establish myriad-household offices administering soldiers and civilians, thereby making fully clear his intention to integrate soldiers with farmers. Regulations were promulgated at the Imperial University, so that scholars knew what they must observe; military authority issued from the court, so that generals could not appropriate it for themselves. In their thoroughness and precision, these arrangements bore comparison without shame to those of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. Moreover, he repeatedly spoke of governing principles and social customs. 是故唐虞三代之政，因革得其宜而可以行於後者也。漢唐宋蓋嘗忽之，而我祖宗列聖則集其大成之妙矣。陛下誠能游心於千古之上，事必考諸已試，動皆求其可師，退然無一毫自是之念，則非徒法唐虞三代，而實所以法我祖宗列聖也。將見聖心洞然，仰有以窺治平之故，俯有以探喪亂之原，真知夫離合之情，灼見夫損益之變，政可通於衆志，法可宜於土俗，而謂因革之宜乃後有昧焉者乎？

紀綱風俗之序，秩然不可紊，而實本於君心者也。唐虞三代具有成績，而我祖宗列聖又得其心法之傳矣。
translation_en:
…the foundation. If what one harbors within is not the mind of Yao and Shun, yet one wishes to achieve the governance of Yao and Shun in administering affairs, this cannot be attained.” How great are these royal words! Do they not truly grasp what is meant by examining antiquity and setting the foundation right? From this, what Your Majesty ought to do becomes clear.

Thus, the government of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties struck the proper balance between retaining and changing institutions, and could be put into practice in later ages. The Han, Tang, and Song neglected this, but our founding ancestors and successive sage sovereigns brought it to consummate fulfillment. If Your Majesty can truly let your thoughts range over the distant past, examine every undertaking against what has already been tried, and in every action seek what can serve as a model, remaining humble without the slightest thought of your own infallibility, then you will be emulating not merely Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, but indeed our founding ancestors and successive sage sovereigns. We shall then see Your Majesty’s mind become thoroughly clear: looking upward, you will discern the causes of orderly and peaceful rule; looking downward, you will probe the origins of ruin and disorder. You will truly understand the circumstances of division and unity and clearly perceive the changes wrought by reducing or adding to institutions. Your policies will accord with the aspirations of the people, and your laws will suit local customs. Could anyone then say that you remained unclear about the proper balance between retaining and changing institutions?

The ordering of the governing framework and of social customs is systematic and must not be confused; its true foundation lies in the ruler’s mind. Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties all had proven achievements, and our founding ancestors and successive sage sovereigns also inherited the transmitted principles for cultivating that mind.

punctuated: 陛下誠能歛此心於一腔之中，戒謹恐懼以全天理之正，省察克治以遏人欲之私，確然無一毫他岐之惑，則非徒學堯舜禹湯文武，而實所以學我祖宗列聖也。將見聖心湛然，皇極以建，儀則以端，躬行之所得真可以顯設於朝廷，平章之所推真可以弘敷於薄海，而謂先後之序乃復有紊焉者乎？夫惟因革之宜既無所昧，則由是推無不準，動無不化，而民用以和。所謂庶績咸熈，百揆時叙，以至位天地、育萬物，而彼和氣之未應，固可以無勞宵旰之憂矣。先後之序既無所紊，則由是紀綱益振，風俗益醇，而民罔不中。所謂正心以正朝廷，正朝廷以正百官，百官正，四方遠近莫不一於正，而彼績效之未臻，亦可以無厪九重之慮矣。若乃舍乎古以為不足法，舍其心以為不足事，則監觀之資已疎，本原之地不立，固非陛下之所當為，而愚臣亦豈敢以為獻哉？雖然，稽諸
translation_en:
If Your Majesty can truly gather this mind within your breast, remaining watchful and apprehensive so as to preserve the correctness of heavenly principle, examining yourself and overcoming your faults so as to restrain the selfishness of human desires, and standing firm without the slightest confusion from divergent paths, then you will not merely be learning from Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu: you will indeed be learning from our dynastic ancestors and successive sage emperors. We shall then see Your Majesty’s mind clear and tranquil, the supreme imperial standard established, and the norms of conduct set right. What you attain through personal practice can truly be made manifest at court, and what you extend through discerning governance can truly be spread throughout the realm. Could anyone then say that the proper order of precedence would again be confused?
Once you fully understand what should appropriately be retained or changed, everything you extend from this understanding will accord with the proper standard, every action will bring transformation, and the people will thereby live in harmony. This is what is meant by “all undertakings flourish, and the hundred affairs are duly ordered,” extending even to “Heaven and Earth taking their proper places and the myriad things being nurtured.” The failure of harmonious influences to respond need surely no longer burden you with anxieties from before dawn until late at night. Once the proper order of precedence is free from confusion, the guiding principles of government will become ever stronger, customs ever purer, and none of the people will fail to attain the mean. This is what is meant by “rectifying the mind to rectify the court, rectifying the court to rectify the hundred officials; when the hundred officials are upright, all throughout the four quarters, far and near, are united in rectitude.” The failure of practical results to be fully realized need likewise no longer trouble Your Majesty within the palace.
But if one abandons antiquity, deeming it unworthy of emulation, and neglects the mind, deeming it unworthy of attention, then the resources for reflective examination become scant, and the foundation is not established. This is certainly not what Your Majesty ought to do; how could your foolish servant dare offer such advice? Nevertheless, examining …

title: 嘉靖二年進士登科錄
text:
古以驗夫因革之宜端其本以不紊先後之序
此亦
陛下今日所已行者特願有以保其終而已耳保之
何如親賢臣以資啓沃之功學古訓以長見聞
之益謹之於一念方萌之初察之於一物未交
之際必使自身而家而國而天下凡有所為輒
與成憲會而後足以言稽古之極不然不可以
自棄也必使由顯而微由鉅而細隨其所在常
與天理俱而後足以言端本之極不然不可以
自肆也昧爽丕顯如成湯之日新始終典學如

punctuated: 古，以驗夫因革之宜；端其本，以不紊先後之序。此亦陛下今日所已行者，特願有以保其終而已耳。保之何如？親賢臣，以資啓沃之功；學古訓，以長見聞之益。謹之於一念方萌之初，察之於一物未交之際。必使自身而家而國而天下，凡有所為，輒與成憲會，而後足以言稽古之極；不然，不可以自棄也。必使由顯而微，由鉅而細，隨其所在，常與天理俱，而後足以言端本之極；不然，不可以自肆也。昧爽丕顯，如成湯之日新；始終典學，如高宗之時敏。則夫紹復祖宗之舊，以上追隆古之治，將必於是焉得之，而所謂勵精有為，亦無要於此者矣。臣愚不勝拳拳，干冒天威，無任惶懼隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en: …antiquity, to determine what should appropriately be retained or changed; and set the foundation right, so that the proper order of precedence is not confused. These are also things Your Majesty is already doing today. My sole wish is that you sustain them to the end. How should they be sustained? Draw close to worthy ministers, benefiting from their enlightening counsel; study the teachings of antiquity, expanding your knowledge and understanding. Exercise care at the very first stirring of a thought, and scrutiny before encountering any external thing. From your own person to your family, the state, and all under Heaven, everything you undertake must accord with established precedents: only then can you be said to have fully realized the study of antiquity. Until then, you must not abandon your efforts. From the manifest to the subtle, from the great to the minute, wherever your attention falls, you must always remain in accord with heavenly principle: only then can you be said to have fully realized the rectification of the foundation. Until then, you must not give yourself free rein. Let your virtue shine forth at dawn, like Cheng Tang’s daily self-renewal; constantly devote yourself to learning from beginning to end, like Gaozong’s unremitting diligence. Through this, you will surely succeed in carrying on and restoring the ancestral institutions, thereby attaining the good government of high antiquity. For what is called exerting oneself wholeheartedly to accomplish something, nothing is more essential than this. Your ignorant servant cannot restrain his earnest devotion. In presuming to offend Your Majesty’s heavenly authority, I am overcome with fear and trembling, to the point of collapse. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.
